MR. MCCLEAVE-ALLEGED FAILURE BY POSTMASTER GENERAL TO GIVE COMPLETE INFORMATION CONCERNING COAT OF ARMS
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege respecting the right of all hon. members of this house to receive proper information in answer to questions presented by them to ministers, or in the course of statements made by ministers on motions.
My question of privilege arises out of remarks of the Postmaster General reported on pages 9063 and 9064 of Hansard for Tuesday last dealing with symbols used by the Canadian post office. At one point the minister said:
Notwithstanding the practice in the past, it is my view that the latest proposal-
That is, the proposal for a symbol
-is a matter of such a nature as to require cabinet approval.
Later, he said:
I think I made it clear that the object of the proposed new symbol now under consideration is merely to provide a symbol of the post office which would be uniform for postal purposes.
I wish to emphasize the use of the words "proposed new symbol".
In Halifax recently, and perhaps in other parts of Canada, post office employees have been delivering a document which I hold in my hand, headed "An apartment number is a necessary part of a postal address". At the bottom of the document appear the words "Issued by authority of the Postmaster General" and alongside the word "General" appears a modernized form of what I presume to be a maple leaf with the initials C. and P intertwined.
I think it was fair to interpret the remarks of the Postmaster General in this house a few days ago as meaning that while changes were being considered, they would first have to go before the cabinet and that in any event they had not as yet been approved. Yet this is the fait accompli with which we have been presented.

Under provisions of the convention of the Universal Postal Union, Christmas cards posted unsealed and bearing conventional formulas of greetings expressed in five words or five initials at the most are classified as "printed matter" and subject to the postage rate applicable to this category of mail.
As far as letters going to Britain, our printed matter rate is 4 cents for the first two ounces and 2 cents for each additional two ounces, which is our general international printed matter rate based on the charges prescribed in the Universal Postal Union Convention. I can add that the special arrangements between Canada and Britain relative to preferential postage rates cover only letters, post cards and second class matter. These rates apply also to every other country in the world except the ones that belong to the Postal Union of the Americas and Spain. Thus, an ordinary Christmas card posted unsealed is subject to a postage rate of 3 cents, which is the general rate in effect in our domestic service for printed matter.

The concern that was expressed in the television interview appears to have been based on a misunderstanding and the misapplication of the regulations made pursuant to the Atomic Energy Control Act, which are intended to limit the exposure of a person to ionizing radiation from radioactive materials during any period of 13 weeks. First, I should like to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre for yielding the floor to me. I intend to be very brief. Indeed, I must necessarily be brief. I shall give the minister of defence a chance to regroup his forces, and, maybe, to set up another line of defence, because the subject with which I am primarily concerned is the proposed route of the new gas pipe line.
I rise to take part in this debate with a deep feeling of frustration because it would seem that my words, or any words spoken by hon. members in this section of the house, will be to no avail, and that the subject matter is closed and finalized as far as the government is concerned. We are faced, so to speak, with a fait accompli.
I am referring, of course, to the routing of the proposed new gas pipe line. I would be a poor representative of northern Ontario if I did not register a strong protest over the way in which this matter has been handled. I was most interested to receive a brief from the Lakehead Industrial Commission suggesting an alternative to the United States route which, to my way of thinking, is a very logical one. Some indication of the probable cost is given in this brief and it would appear that a Canadian route would cost more money-about $35 million more than the United States route. But the question which arises is this: is the spending of another $35 million or even $50 million of such importance in connection with a project such as this when all the other factors are taken into consideration? First of all, there is the huge expenditure which would accrue in Canada on wages and on materials during construction. I think this is an item which multiplies itself many times when one considers the impact of a scheme such as this upon the whole economic picture.
Second, we should take into account the additional employment which would be provided in connection with the maintenance of the pipe line. It is not just a matter of the

November 1, 1966
Interim Supply
wages involved; there are personal and corporate taxes which would have to be paid, and these would also be part of the total economic picture for many years to come.
The third consideration we should bear in mind is probably the most important: Canada would have complete control over a tremendously important natural resource. It would seem to me that if a portion of the line were built through the United States, that portion would definitely come under the jurisdiction of the United States Federal Power Commission. I do not think there can be any argument about that; I believe we would lose control over that portion of the line.
I have heard a great deal about the size of this pipe line. We have been told that the size is not a matter of great importance, but that it is the pressure which makes the difference. I should like the committee to consider the example I am about to give. Take a water line, for instance. A line an inch in diameter will certainly carry much more water than a half inch line under the same pressure. So it seems only common sense to suggest that a 36-inch line would carry a great deal more gas than a smaller line.
The Lakehead Industrial Commission proposes the construction of a line which would run parallel to the present line, cut through Fort Frances and reach the lakehead by that route. It would then "twin" the line from the lakehead north of Nipigon, pass through Nipigon, go through Terrace Bay and Marathon to the "Sault". Along the north shore of Lake Superior there is a great potential for the sale of natural gas. There are a great number of pulp and paper mills. There is a tremendous area ready for development, an area which is rich in iron ore. In the Wawa area in particular there is room for expansion, and the same applies to the Manitou-wadge area farther north. I believe that if gas were made available in these areas there would certainly be a great deal of expansion in the mining industry throughout the region, not just at those points I have mentioned.
From Sault Ste. Marie the proposed line would go to Sudbury, and at Sudbury it could be "junctioned" to provide extra gas for Quebec. It could also be routed south, and if there is a sale for gas across the line, as no doubt there is, why could this gas not be taken across the border at Sault Ste. Marie or, for that matter, at Fort Frances?

If natural gas were made available in this area, the cost of processing the ore would, I believe, be reduced to such an extent that it would be possible to pay freights charges on an economic basis. a (3:40 p.m.)
If it were feasible for the iron ore to be developed and pelletized at a reasonable cost, then I think we could be assured that devel-lopment in the Nakina area would go ahead. This is something which is important for northern Ontario because, as most hon. members realize, Nakina is, shall we say, a doomed community. It will only be a matter of time until the main industry in the town, which is the Canadian National Railways, will be moved away from there. The community hospital, the composite schools and various other public enterprises require a large community to support them, and it would mean a great deal to the whole area if Nakina were permitted to survive. This, I suggest, is one of the ways that that could be done.
I frankly admit that the Sudbury area is serviced with gas, but there is continuing expansion taking place there. International Nickel is spending a large amount of money to enlarge its plant at Copper Cliff, and with all this new expansion there will be a need for a greater supply of gas. The whole Sudbury basin is going through a period of development and expansion, and if it should happen that a shortage of gas resulted in curtailment of this expansion it would be a serious thing, not only for Sudbury and northern Ontario, but also for the economy as a whole.
Perhaps I may be getting a little political when I say that we in northern Ontario are becoming a bit tired of all the platitudes about the potential of the great north; about it being the source of our mineral supplies and requiring development. Here is an example where expansion in the north could be given new impetus. But instead of providing the north with the services it needs, the new gas supply will be going across the border where it will help industries there to compete, not only with our northern industries but with the whole iron ore industry of Canada.
November 1, 1966

I am limited as to time, Mr. Chairman, so I shall not spend any more on this subject. In conclusion, I hope that if it is at all possible reconsideration will be given to this matter, and I heartily recommend the submission of the Lakehead Industrial Commission as a pattern for development with regard to the new pipe line across Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I want to take part in this debate on the subject of national defence because I think it is one of the most important subjects-

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman yielded his place to the hon. member for Nickel Belt. I wish to point out that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has another engagement later this evening and would like to speak at this time in reply to some of the points raised yesterday. In the circumstances I wonder if my hon. friend and you, Mr. Chairman, would agree to let him speak at this time.
How long will your speech be?

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the reason for asking this privilege is that tonight the Canadian government is host at a dinner in Montreal for the delegates to the water pollution conference, and if possible I would like to be there at six o'clock.
If the minister would limit his remarks to 12 minutes I would willingly agree. If not, he can follow me.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member yielded his place. Surely, there is no reason why we should not hear from the minister now.
The minister is trying to get autocratic again. I think I will go ahead with what I want to say.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The minister can come back tomorrow; the issue will still be alive.

Exactly; that is a profound statement and I agree with it. Both issues that have been before the house will still be alive. Certainly, the issue of national defence will still be alive, because I do not know of any problem of greater concern to the people *of the country than that of national defence.
If we continue this debate then hon. members will get the significance of this issue. The people of Canada will get the significance of it, and it may even be that C.B.C.
Interim Supply
radio and television will begin to understand what is going on here in the House of Commons. Once the C.B.C. gets L.B.J. home from Korea and Alaska, and keeps us fully informed which governor in the United States is going to be affected by the backlash, and once it gets the political situation in Germany settled to its satisfaction, then perhaps it will draw to the attention of the Canadian people a serious situation right here in the House of Commons and right here in Canada.
Hear, hear.

I do not know of any graver
charge made against the Minister of National Defence than was made yesterday by the five hon. gentlemen who spoke on this subject, the hon. member for Calgary North, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, the junior hon. member for Halifax, the hon. member for Peace River and the hon. member for Greenwood. Each one in turn made charges against the minister. They charged him with irresponsibility and with failing to give full information to the house.
I would say this to you, Mr. Chairman, that this minister runs the gravest risk of having a charge made against him in the house, not only of misleading the house but of knowingly and deliberately misleading the house. I do not know of any more serious charge that may be laid against a minister of the crown.
Let me point out what happened here yesterday. In the space of just five minutes when I was present I made notes of the speech made by the hon. member for Calgary North, with respect to the charges he made. You can find the first one at page 9310 of yesterday's Hansard, where he is recorded as saying:
-the Canadian public is paying more for defence and getting much less of it.
That is the opposite to what the Minister of National Defence has been telling the house.
Hear, hear.

On the same page of
Hansard, in reference to the minister, the hon. member for Calgary North said this:
He has been attempting to go ahead with that unification in spite of the fact that there has been no parliamentary approval for it. and in effect has been attempting to present us with a fait accompli.
That is charge number two which I casually picked out.
As recorded at page 9311 the hon. member for Calgary North was talking about antisubmarine capability. The minister has stated

November 1, 1966
Interim Supply
over and over again that it is greater now than it has ever been at any time in the past, but the hon. member for Calgary North said:
It does not take an expert to know that this statement is not correct. It just cannot possibly be correct.
These are serious charges against the minister. On the question of how much money was being spent on equipment, the hon. member for Calgary North said, as recorded at page 9312 of Hansard:
Last year, as a matter of fact, I think the minister spent a smaller proportion on equipment than in many years past, about 12 per cent.
That is not the impression that the minister is giving to the public.
As recorded at page 9313 of Hansard the hon. member for Calgary North said:
He is thus trying to cover up a completely irresponsible action in suppressing evidence.
The hon. member was referring to the evidence of Admiral Landymore that was suppressed by the minister. His speech contained five serious charges, and I could And more in it. Similar serious charges were made by the other members who spoke yesterday.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
No more serious charge was made than that made by the hon. member for Peace River who showed that the minister, by his action, was destroying the committee system of this house. He was doing this by tampering with evidence and preventing people called before the committee from giving the evidence the committee required in order to form a judgment. The hon. member for Peace River showed very clearly that he was talking about facts that the committees require. He was not talking about witnesses making statements with regard to policy. Now, these are serious matters. The Minister of National Defence is quoted in the papers as having snapped back at his critics. Let us have recorded in the news media the charges made against this minister, and we will see how much snapping back he will do which will carry any weight at all. The minister is under a very serious cloud. He has been asked questions day after day and week after week. Charges have been made against him on a question of privilege, and he has not cleared his name. We are going to give him an opportunity this week to do just that, and to show to the Canadian people just what is going on in the national defence department. I hope we can smoke him out before this week is over and find out from him what exactly his policy is.

Let us find out whether the minister's policy is to destroy the army, the navy and the air force. Let us find out whether his policy is to put all these men in one uniform, or whether his policy is to reduce the size of our forces, and if so to what figure. This is the information we certainly require. Is he going to go on blandly informing us and the people, through various agents he has, that everything is fine and that we have a better force than we ever had in the past. I intend by actual figures to show that the situation is not as clear and rosy as the minister tries to show.
Let us look at the picture over the last three years. In 1963 the Liberal government set up a committee on defence. You would have thought it was the only committee on defence which ever had been set up. They made it a standing committee, and it may meet now each session. It should be meeting right now in the fall of this year, but we are blocked at every turn when we ask for the re-assembly of that committee. The minister does not want it re-assembled because he cannot stand the type of evidence which would come before the committee and the exposure to which he would be subjected if that committee met and had the privilege of calling outside witnesses to appear before it.
When the Prime Minister was dealing with this subject in 1963, it was the calling of outside witnesses to appear before that committee which he mentioned. Of course the Prime Minister said that the committee, if it has serving officers or officials of the departments in front of it, will not question them with regard to	policy-with which I
agree-but will have the opportunity to question them with regard to facts. I should like to refer to Hansard, 1963, volume I, May 30, page 458. The Prime Minister's words are as follows:
It is also provided in the resolution that the committee, if it so desires, can send for outside witnesses. By that I mean witnesses who would not be serving officers of the armed forces or civil serants of the government of Canada, who would naturally appear before the committee only to give information in regard to matters of fact. But outside witnesses whom the committee felt by their knowledge and experience could contribute to the work of the committee would, it seems to me, be very appropriate witnesses for the committee to summon if it so desired.
That is exactly what we want at this stage. We want the outside witnesses. We know that the witnesses which would be provided from the defence services themselves would be hampered and restrained now by the Minister
November 1, 1966

-of National Defence. He will examine the [DOT]evidence they propose to give and will strike out things which he does not want made public. But, let us get some of the outside witnesses; let us examine some of these officers who have been removed from the services because they would not go along with the minister's policy. Let us have these witnesses in front of us and let them tell us how it happened that they resigned, retired or were fired from the services, and the reasons therefor.
We have had a serious depletion of experienced men in the three services, men who have spent a lifetime in learning their trade, the professional sailors, soldiers and airmen. These are the men we want to appear before us. Let them tell us just what has happened. Let us have their views with regard to the policy of the minister. When we were discussing the seating up of that standing committee on May 30, 1963, I used these words as recorded at page 463 of Hansard of that date:
What happens when the committee is discussing some matter dealing with defence policy and discovers that the decision has already been made by the government?
I asked a second question:
What will happen if during the course of this committee the government is faced with some problem relating to defence on which a decision is required? Will that be referred to the committee for consideration before the government makes its decision-
In the course of the debate in 1963 the minister was arguing that we could discuss policy. Well, that was a sham and a delusion, because when we were discussing or attempting to discuss policy in the house committee on defence in 1963-and I was then a member-we were faced with this situation: We were discussing the navy and the program of shipbuilding with regard to frigates. While we were in the course of that discussion the minister issued an order that the frigate program be discontinued. He did not tell the committee that this was going to happen. He just proceeded to discontinue the building program for frigates and left the committee in mid air.
On October 8, 1963, just before this happened, I asked him a question as recorded on page 332 of the committee reports:
-does the minister now want the committee to make a recommendation to him with regard to the naval program?
The minister replied that that was not necessary. He said:
I think a decision will be taken shortly and it will be announced just as soon at it is taken.
Interim Supply
Then Mr. Smith, a member of the committee, said:
Then why do we not adjourn now?
I must say that that was a very sensible suggestion. A few minutes later the hon. member for Vancouver East, at page 334 said:
My other question is perhaps out of date now in view of the minister's statement that he does not want any advice on the navy.
There we were misled by the minister and the Prime Minister. This committee was blazoned as a committee to discuss defence policy, and the minister wanted no advice whatsoever from the committee. He would announce the policy and if we wanted to discuss it afterward, well and good, but not otherwise. He did a similar thing to us with regard to the reserve forces. He set up a committee to study the reserve forces and removed any hope for consideration by the committee of this matter. He went ahead, made his decision, cut down the reserve forces, and we were permitted to discuss the matter after it had been done.
From 1963 on the minister has been acting in this fashion. He has been pretending that the committee on national defence is a useful assistant to him. He has said publicly that the committee may discuss policy, and he has created the impression that the committee will influence his decisions with regard to national defence. At the same time, he is carrying on and making decisions without asking the advice of the committee. He completely ignores the advice of the committee when it tries to offer advice and, as we now have found out, has tampered with the evidence that witnesses gave to that committee.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
One of the reasons I withdrew from the defence committee after that 1963 session was the attitude of the minister. I realized that it was futile to attempt to do anything to influence his decisions because he had made up his mind and, in the face of professional advice and evidence, was determined stubbornly to go his own way. I think he had been busy reading "The Making of a President" to see how things were accomplished in the United States, in order that he could move ahead politically.
The next step was the presentation of a white paper on defence in 1964, and the debate in 1964 on amendments to the National Defence Act which did away with the chiefs of staff committee and appointed one man in

November 1, 1966
Interim Supply
charge, the chief of defence staff. We opposed that move as vigorously as we could. We discussed the white paper and pointed out its deficiencies. It was our suggestion that it was wrong to go back to an outmoded system and appoint just one man in charge, a "supremo", and attempt to conduct national defence policy under those circumstances.
I will not quote my own words again because I have already done so too often, but it was our suggestion at that time that if we had a minister of defence and a chief of staff who were in disagreement one or the other would have to go. We suggested that if we had a minister of national defence and a chief of staff who were always in agreement this must mean that either the minister or the chief of staff was a puppet. When you have two men and one is of an extremely strong character, or very stubborn, then the other would have to be an agent or a puppet. In the circumstances what would happen when the minister was changed, as he will be some day? If the chief of staff was a strong man then the minister of national defence would be a puppet in the hands of that chief of staff.
It is my hope that our serving soldiers, sailors and airmen who have reached high ranks, many of whom have seen active service and served their country well, will not be subjected to the control and authority exercised by this Minister of National Defence. I think it would be humiliating to place men who have seen active service under the authority of this minister and make them just water boys.
At this time the present minister has his senior officers travelling around the country selling his ideas with regard to integration, and his ideas with regard to a common uniform for all service personnel. Why are they not dealing with the efficiency of our services? Why are they not insisting that the navy be restored to its former position? Why are they not insisting that infantry battalions be brought up to strength? Surely, that is their job. Why are they not dealing with the really serious matter of morale within the service? Instead of doing these things, they are travelling as spokesmen for the minister in an attempt to sell his policies.
They were also out during the election campaign.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Do not be bitter.

There is something seriously wrong with policy when a minister has to depend upon his senior serving officers to sell it to the public of this country. I think our senior officers have a duty far and above their duty to this temporary civilian head of the department. These senior officers owe a duty to the people of this country, because we are relying on these trained experienced men to maintain our fighting forces in good shape. We are relying on them to look after the young men who enter these forces, so that if they are called upon to risk their lives they will do so under circumstances which will be somewhat advantageous.
You can rely on them.

I hope that I can rely on these senior serving officers, but I can place no reliance at all on the Minister of National Defence. The minister gave the whole story away last night. He has been talking for three years about what he calls the savings he is going to effect in our defence budget. He told us early in 1963 about the $100 million he intended to save in the national defence budget. I succeeded in getting him to change his words when I pointed out to him that this would not actually be a saving but a transfer of funds within the national defence budget. He was attempting to tell us, and sell the people of this country, the false information that he was saving money and creating greater efficiency in the forces.
Last night the minister gave the game away. All along, for three years, he has said that as a result of integration there would be this transfer of funds and that we would have more funds for equipment. The hon. member for Calgary North pointed out the complete failure along those lines. The minister has told us that through integration, and as a result of other policies, he would have extra money for other purposes. Last night he told us that this was the result of a reduction in the strength of our forces, including a reduction of 7,000 civilians. He has reduced the forces by 23,000 and he says the savings amount to $150 million. He also suggests that we have a more efficient force as a result. During the 30 odd seconds I spoke last night, I pointed out that if he reduced our forces by another 23,000 this year he could save another $150 million, but that if he repeated this each year we would eventually entirely cut out defence spending and would end up with no army, navy or air force.
November 1, 1966

One can easily see how the minister has misled the people of Canada. He suggested that integration had accomplished a savings when in fact any savings effected were the result of the reduction of personnel within the armed forces. He told us in 1964 that his objective was a reduction of 10,000 armed forces personnel. At that time we had 120,000 in our armed forces. He has now cut that strength down by over 20,000. How misleading can this man be?
You better get your statistics straightened out.

The minister now tells me that I should get my statistics straightened out. Let me tell him that I was quoting from the minister's words, and from the minutes of the proceedings of the national defence committee. I invite the minister to give us some statistics upon which we can place some reliance.
Mr. Chairman, I cannot in 30 minutes begin to cover the various things that must eventually be said on this occasion. I will give the house a rest from my words, and later on today or tomorrow present some more information. In the five minutes I have left, let me deal with one or two other matters. I warn the minister not to think that I do not intend to deal at some length with unification when the time comes, and with the subject of Admiral Landymore's evidence when that opportunity presents itself.
At this time I should like to pay the highest tribute possible to Admiral Lan-dymore for the public service he has performed. I know enough about serving officers to realize how reluctant they are to get into the field of political life, and to realize that the course of their lives over 20 or 30 years is devoted to carrying out orders and performing their duties. Naturally, as a result, they hesitate to plunge into the maelstrom of political life. Admiral Landymore performed a service to the people of Canada when he stated his position, yet he was fired by the Minister of National Defence on July 12. It was on July 15 that he made his public statement.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Last night the minister attempted to tell us-he misled us again-that Admiral Landymore made his public statement when he was still under orders not to do it. But he had been told on the 12th that he was fired; that the paperwork had to go through because it had to be posted and this, that and
Interim Supply
the other thing. Admiral Landymore deserves the thanks of the people of Canada for exposing what the minister is attempting to do to our armed services, and particularly with regard to the navy.
Hear, hear.

Let me just deal with the strength of the navy at the present time. Three years ago 60 ships were operated by our navy. Now, we are down to 23. Admiral Landymore points out that unless recruitment for the navy is stepped-up we will be down to about 13 ships in the spring of 1967. Yet the minister tells us that our navy is in better shape than it was three years ago.
Some of the ships are old and have to be retired and replaced. Admiral Landymore pointed out that there will be a six-year gap before the new ships are ready, because there was a very serious delay by the minister in placing the orders for the keels to be laid. What do we do in that six-year gap? The minister says he will not keep some of the older ships in commission; recruitment for the navy has dropped to an all-time low, and so our navy will become very small indeed by the spring of 1967. Yesterday the junior member for Halifax stated that he had the report that the chief of staff had forecast that within five years the navy would be nonexistent, except for transport purposes. That is the future that faces us with regard to the navy, and I think it is a very serious matter indeed.
Let the minister tell us what is the strength of the army. On June 8 of this year, as reported at page 6132 of Hansard, in answer to a question by the hon. member for York-Sunbury the minister replied:
Canada has twelve infantry battalions and one anti-tank infantry battalion. On 30 April, 1966, eight infantry battalions and the anti-tank battalion (less one detached company with the Canadian brigade group in Germany) were serving in Canada; three infantry battalions were serving overseas with the Canadian brigade group; and one infantry battalion was serving in Cyprus.
The total strength of the 13 battalions on 30 April, 1966, was 8,718.
That gives an average strength for a battalion of 670 all ranks, and the establishment calls for a strength of 857 and upward for all ranks. Every infantry battalion, on the average, is under strength. So it is not only the navy that has suffered from this decline in recruitment and this hasty removal of personnel; the army itself has suffered. If the minister were called upon to provide two or

November 1, 1966-
Interim Supply
three battalions for overseas duty somewhere, he would have to start making transfers from other battalions within Canada to bring them up to strength.

Now
tell them what a battalion is.
Oh, oh.

This is the result of the minister's policy. He intends, apparently, to wipe out the navy; the army is now under strength, and the air force is designed for just a transport role. The minister claims that he is saving the taxpayers' money and, in order to do that, is reducing the strength of Canada's armed forces. This is his policy: he is going to put the whole group together into one single force and in one uniform. I do not know what we will have by the time he has finished.
The minister has not given the house the information that we should have had over all these months. I intend, Mr. Chairman, to quote chapter and verse pointing out the evasion of the minister and the misleading statements he has made to the house which show that he is incompetent to hold his present position.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should first like to apologize for my absence yesterday; however, I think it was justified. On Sunday, I had the opportunity to speak to the members of the Independent Petroleum Association of America. Some of those present also did not look too favourably upon the project of the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Company Ltd. but, of course, for different reasons than those of some of the members in this house.
Yesterday in Montreal I was at the opening of the conference on water pollution and, this morning, I was part of a group of ministers who welcomed a delegation from Nova Scotia.
This explains why I did not study yesterday's debate in depth. I may overlook some of the arguments set forth or leave uncorrected some of the possible mistakes in speeches made by some of my hon. colleagues.
Before going into the proposal in detail, I should like to submit three or four general comments to the house.
The first one is somewhat philosophical; it deals with the very nature of the government. It has often been said that to govern
lMr. Churchill.]
is to foresee. It should be added that to govern is to choose. Mr. Chairman, very seldom is that choice made between good and evil. An English author named Burke, very close to the party opposite, claimed that "to govern is to choose among inconveniences." Such a choice is therefore not made between good and evil; in every decision made, there are always good and bad points.
Mention has been made earlier of the brief submitted by the Lakehead Industrial Commission, but it must be kept in mind that in its brief, that organization actually points out the advantages and disadvantages of the project now under discussion.
The commission concluded that the disadvantages were greater than the advantages while the government concluded that the advantages were greater than the disadvantages. But both parties weighed the pros and cons before reaching such a decision and it is a matter of judgment or as you would say in English, Mr. Chairman, "most of these decisions are taken on balance."
Those decisions have also been reached by the government taking into account the overall interests of the country. It is obvious that they will displease certain areas of the country even sometimes for the wrong reasons, as I will have the opportunity to explain it later.
But again, it is with the interest of Canada as a whole in mind that the central government must make decisions such as the one made in this case.
My second remark, Mr. Chairman, is to say that a government decision must deal with an existing project. Such project might very properly be compared with other projects that might exist. Indeed, the National Energy Board did compare this project of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to one which might exist, that is the twinning of the northern Ontario pipe line. But, in the end, the government must render a decision on something concrete, on something that exists and not on something which might exist in the future. Those decisions must be made now. It is very well to bring forward other alternatives at this time, but we would like to know who exactly is ready to implement such alternatives.
I also wish to submit that this project is presented to us by an honourable company. I do not feel we are justified in questioning its intentions.
November 1, 1966

The hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) criticized Trans-Canada Pipe Lines yesterday, but I think he was referring to the wrong company and that he meant the Northern Ontario Natural Gas Company. I feel this point is worthy of note and we must also remember that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited is just as much Canadian as anyone here, that 92 per cent of its shareholders are Canadians. And I do not feel we are justified in systematically questioning this company's sincerity as some members tried to do yesterday, if I interpreted their comments correctly.
We must also take into consideration the fact that this project is supported by several provincial governments, several natural gas producers associations, by natural gas distributing companies, several members of the house, several well-known members of the economic press and, I suppose even by several supporters of the N.D.P. throughout the country. Therefore, this is no hoax presented by the government. This is a very serious matter, it is a project which has the support of a very great number of people who know their business.
The government is often confronted with newspaper articles disapproving of its policies. I find it quite strange that it is so seldom quoted in favourable articles. I believe that, in the present case, several qualified members of the press admitted that the new project, as presented, as approved, was a great deal better than the first one. Some writers even felt that the first project was very valid and that the government should have approved of it.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
But there is one fundamental aspect which we must take into account. This project, this program, this Great Lakes Pipe Line project has the support the National Energy Board which has legal jurisdiction in this field, whose controlling authority is quasi-judicial and it is, moreover, the advisory authority in the matter, having at its disposal the specialized technical and economic apparatus enabling it to evaluate this type of situation.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Dief-enbaker) blames the government for not having followed the advice of the National Energy Board and, at the same time, accuses us of selling our country to the United States. I suggest that he should make up his mind, because the National Energy Board has clearly approved of this project.
Interim Supply
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) said that, in view of the fact that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited had been incorporated by an act of parliament, it was up to the parliament to decide on the worthiness of the project before us at the present time. I do not believe I am distorting his line of thought in saying this.
It must be pointed out at this time that Canadian companies operating interprovincial and international gas or oil pipe lines, have all been incorporated by a special act of parliament. Indeed, section 25 says that:
No person other than a company shall construct or operate a pipe line.
And the definition of "company" is given in section 2 (Q) which reads as follows:
"Special Act" means an act of the parliament of Canada authorizing a person named in the act to construct or operate a pipe line.
Thus, this is not an unusal case; indeed it is the general case in all existing situations.
Thus, Trans-Canada Pipe Lines created in 1951 is given by that special act powers to construct and operate pipe lines. Now, it is the duty of the National Energy Board, under the act authorizing them to do so, to grant licences and permits, within the framework of the general legislation, taking into consideration the acts creating the said companies.
The only thing peculiar to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Ltd. is section 6, paragraph (a) which reads, if my memory serves me right, as follows:
"Trans-Canada Pipe Lines agrees to build its main pipe line or lines in Canada."
That is the only special aspect of that incorporating act. Now, in 1957 and 1958 the company built a pipe line which is its main pipe line. The company now undertakes, by a formal agreement signed with the Canadian government, to respect that situation.
In effect, the agreement signed by the company and the government, which agreement I tabled in the house Friday, will ensure that "The main pipe line of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited will remain in Canada."
I really cannot see what is wrong with that agreement. I feel that we have respected the law in this case.

So, the main pipe line of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited will remain in Canada.
