speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: That is exactly what I suggest. I am saying that if the company wants to do something other than it committed itself to parliament to do in 1951, it should come back to parliament again. That is precisely what I am saying.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: On this matter of pipe lines, all other special acts of parliament give the companies which have these special acts the right to build pipe lines within or outside of Canada. This provision, therefor, would be redundant. Unless the intentions of parliament was not to give this company the advantages that it has given other companies. There is no reason to do this, even if I were to accept the hon. member's interpretation of the law, which I do not.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Does the minister contend that the phrase "within or outside Canada" in the opening part of section 6 (a) of the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Act covers the building of pipe lines outside of Canada? Has he read the evidence given before the railways, canals and telegraph lines committee in 1951?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, it does cover that and the company already has four other pipe lines connected with United States

pipe lines. So, you will have to make your law retroactive and deprive the company of an advantage that it gained in 1951.

Mr. Chairman, I think we could end this debate very quickly if the minister would remind the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that there was also a committee of parliament which dealt with this matter in 1954, in which committee this matter was thoroughly discussed and decided upon.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I am grateful to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle for letting me have the benefit of his experience and his very intimate knowledge of these matters, which I admit I have not. I have done my homework as well as I know how, but there are elements connected with the history of this problem that still escape me.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: May I ask whether the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Act of 1951 was amended in 1954 or at any other time?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Not to my knowledge, Mr. Chairman, but if it has been I will try to let him know later on in the debate.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: My contention is that if the act is still in force it should be lived up to.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I was saying, Mr. Chairman, that the National Energy Board, which has the respect of everyone in this house and outside it, has made a decision, which was rendered last August. In making that decision the National Energy Board brought to the attention of the government certain matters of public interest, such as the control that the Federal Power Commission would exercise on the transportation of gas from western Canada to eastern Canada, the possible economic disadvantages that might follow the construction of a pipe line through the United States, and so on. The government then looked at these reservations and made a decision, stating that it could not agree with a project that of necessity did not route the main line through Canada. I think this was both in the national interest and in accordance with the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Act.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I apologize for changing from English to French, but my notes are in French and so I shall continue in that language.
November 1, 1966

Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Ltd. answered the objections put forward by the government by offering guarantees, which hon. members know very well and which I shall not enumerate here. There is the guarantee of 50, 60, 65 per cent-everybody knows what I mean-which prevents the company from selling its interest in the Great Lakes project without the consent of the federal government; there is also the guarantee ensuring that the building or looping of the Northern Ontario pipe line will begin in 1970. This agreement was formally set down in a document which may be criticized-it is the privilege of hon. members to do so-but which, in my opinion, offers maximum security. I find it a precise and clearly written document, and it even contains a section, that is section 9, providing for rather severe penalties, since every time the company violates one of its guarantees, it will have to pay a fine of one million dollars.
Consequently, I do not think we can say that the commitment is not serious. I do not want members to think-far from it-that the government lacks confidence in the company by imposing such a heavy penalty, for any breach of its promises.
Hon. members must keep in mind that the National Energy Board will continue to keep watch on the implementation of this project. The company cannot export natural gas without obtaining a permit from the National Energy Board and, consequently, it will have to keep the National Energy Board-this is stated in the formal agreement -informed of its progress, of its transactions.
Therefore, the National Energy Board will thus be in a position to watch over things and inform the government if it feels the company is not fulfilling its obligations entirely.
A third point, Mr. Chairman, to say that, upon reading over yesterday's discussion and comments printed in certain newspapers, along with the observations made by certain associations, I have a feeling that an assumption prevails throughout the debate, and in the mind of some, an assumption which is not openly expressed but which is continuously present in the background. This assumption is that the Canadian government should own and operate the pipeline itself. The answer to that is very simple.
We have in Canada other means of transportation: transportation by radio, by television, by railways, by airplanes, by electricity, in which federal and provincial governments have interests, but where private enterprise
Interim Supply
also has its share. This is a situation of mixed economy, private and public.
We also have in Canada other means of transportation wholly owned by private enterprise, such as highway transportation, water transportation, telephone transportation, as well as interprovincial and international pipe fines. Some of my hon. colleagues in the house would perhaps disagree with this system. They might want the government to take over gradually or at once these means of transportation through nationalization or otherwise.
But, the fact remains that the Canadian people have not yet expressed the wish to change this system thoroughly. If the party which I am thinking about succeeds in convincing the Canadian people of this need, in a very democratic way, we will bow before their decision. At present, I think that, as they are good democrats, they should abide by the will of the Canadian people, who have not yet expressed the opinion that the government should nationalize all these means of communication.
Thus, it is within the framework of the general philosophy existing right now in Canada that this decision has been taken by the government to allow the building of this pipe line.

I was saying a moment ago that quite recently an association called the Lakehead Industrial Commission presented the government with a brief. In the brief, the disadvantages of the project are mentioned. I do not deny that some points raised are quite valid. I will not say that some of these ideas will not be used at a future date. I do not know. I agree that some of the reasoning in the brief makes sense.
As I said ten minutes ago, the association thinks that, on balance, the disadvantages are greater than the advantages. These gentlemen were honest enough, and I congratulate them for that, to mention also the advantages of doing it the way we are. There are indeed some major advantages.
The first advantage, as they stated themselves, would be lower construction costs resulting in lower gas prices in eastern Canada. This fact is adduced in the hearings conducted by the National Energy Board. Trans-Canada's application established that the Great Lakes proposal would make possible the delivery of western Canadian gas to eastern Canada at prices lower than otherwise could be realized. Nobody will deny that.

November 1, 1966
Interim Supply
The reductions may not be as great as some people-myself for example-would have expected. It must be remembered that the National Energy Board stated that these reductions in transmission costs were not as much as had been suggested. The view that there would be reductions in the price of gas in eastern Canada was supported by all the distributors in eastern Canada, including Northern and Central Gas Company which serves the Ontario north.
The greatest advantage would accrue to industrial customers. Consequently, the cheaper gas would encourage industrial development in Quebec and Ontario, including northern Ontario. It is easy to see that what is true for eastern Canada in general is also true for northern Ontario, where we get most of the complaints with respect to this project.
Could I ask the minister a question? Would the minister tell us what saving is involved? What is the comparison in rates between the Great Lakes line and the northern line?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: The Northern and Central Gas Company, the northern Ontario distributor, stated at two National Energy Board hearings that the contract concluded between itself and Trans-Canada contingent on the approval of the Great Lakes project, would result in savings of three cents per thousand cubic feet of gas purchased under the contract compared with prices which would otherwise apply. There is no change in the present price of gas, but there is a reduction of about three cents per thousand cubic feet in the new contract already negotiated between the local company in northern Ontario and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines. So, there is a clear advantage.

Could I ask the minister another question? Were these prices checked and approved by the National Energy Board? The figures do not seem to agree with the figures given by the National Energy Board itself in its report.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: They are part of the report of the National Energy Board, yes.
There is a difference of one fifth of one cent in transmission costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: One fifth of a cent for what?
That is the difference between the rates in transmission costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I am sorry. We might discuss this later on.
The second advantage is the shorter construction time. The original plan envisaged construction of the Great Lakes project in two years. While it is obvious that no construction can take place this year, it is possible that the whole project could be constructed next year. This would obviate further imports of United States gas into Canada, as well as give the advantages of lower costs more rapidly than might otherwise be the case.
The third point the brief mentions has to do with exports. Already 103 million cubic feet of gas for export at Emerson to Midwestern is contingent on the Great Lakes project. Eighty seven million cubic feet are contingent also on the Great Lakes project. These 87 million cubic feet would go to the Michigan and Wisconsin company, through the projected line.
* (4:40 p.m.)
In the letter of August 25 last, the company also stated that American Natural Gas, its partner, agreed to purchase 100 million cubic feet more. The company also stated there was an additional possibility of selling 100 million cubic feet more.
As I said last Friday, the government decision does not rely on these potential exports, though it takes them into consideration. It is quite likely that the National Energy Board would have to approve these further exports with priority given, of course, to the Canadian national interests and to the surplus possibilities.
I do not think anyone disagrees that there is a need to export to the United States. One out of five Canadians lives on the earnings from exports. We export all sorts of things to the United States. We are exporting at the present time $104 million worth of gas. Some people argue that we should not export gas. That argument might be applied equally well to any of the other commodities we are exporting to the United States.
There is no doubt that if we in Canada wish to continue living at the standard to which we have grown accustomed, we need to export a lot. Only by exporting goods can we import others. One hon. member underlined the fear of continentalism. Well, this fear has been with us for 100 years or more, and I presume it will be with us for another 100 years or more. It is something geography dictates. I am often asked, with respect to
November 1, 1966

water, in particular, whether I am a nationalist or a continentalist. I answer, by a pirouette, perhaps, that I would be a continen-tal'ist if it were in the national interest. But this is the kind of decision Canadians have been making for 100 years and which, I venture to suggest, we will be making for 100 years to come.
With respect to financing, the lakehead brief accepts the idea that financing of the Great Lakes project would be easier. At the March, 1966, hearing, Trans-Canada emphasized the difficulty of financing the alternative northern Ontario route, and this difficulty was reiterated in the company's letter of September 26.
It is difficult to estimate precisely the difference in cost between the possible northern loop and the Great Lakes loop. The brief to which I referred mentioned $35 million, but other figures which are available to me suggest a greater difference in cost. Whatever the figure is exactly, nobody denies that the cost of the Great Lakes project would be lower than the likely cost of a northern Ontario loop. Moreover, everybody is aware that it is difficult to borrow money at the present time, and I presume this is one of the considerations which is in the mind of the company and of the government also.
With respect to the looping of the Ontario pipe line in 1970, it seems to me we are gaining an advantage at the moment in the sense that the Great Lakes project is more favourable at this point. Perhaps I am flattering the government too much-and if this should be the case I apologize to members of the committee-when I express the belief that we have protected the long term Canadian interest, by making it necessary for a northern Ontario loop to be constructed, beginning in 1970. Indeed, I might blandly say that we have the best of two worlds, because we have the immediate advantage of the Great Lakes project while maintaining the future advantage of the looping in Canada. This is a real Canadian solution, and I thought it was a rather good one, when we reached it.

May I ask the minister
whether there is any completion date to which the company is committed with reference to this looping of the northern line? There is a commencement date, but is there any completion date?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
No. There could not be one because one would not think of forcing a company to do something which was not
Interim Supply
commercially viable. But the 60 per cent progression is tied to the forecast of sales presented by the company to the National Energy Board and accepted by the board as being rational and possible. Thus, if the growth of markets progresses as the company expects, and as the National Energy Board agrees is possible, then the looping would become necessary in 1970 and it will take place faster or slower depending on the growth of sales. I do not think one can force anybody to do more than that.
Is it not true that the commencement of the loop by 1970 is contingent only upon it being required on the basis of sales?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: No. It is an obligation upon the company to begin looping by 1970.
But only if sales require it?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: No, it is not tied to the forecast. It is absolute. What is tied to the forecast of market growth is the 60 per cent.
Ah, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: The company will begin by 1970. How many miles of pipe line will be looped in 1970, I do not know with precision. It will depend, of course, on the growth of markets in the meantime.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: And upon what time in 1970 they start. They might start on December 31.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. minister, but the time allotted to him has expired.
Is there unanimous consent to enable the minister to continue his remarks?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I will proceed more rapidly from now on. The other favourable argument is connected with safety and security. There is no doubt that a second pipe line would lead to increased safety in the transportation of gas from western to eastern Canada. Of course, some of our lakehead friends will say that a similar element of increased safety would exist if their north shore project was built. Indeed, but I can say also that the construction of a line along the north shore would be more expensive according to everybody's calculations.

November 1, 1966
Interim Supply
There are other advantages which the lake-head brief does not mention. One is the additional capacity immediately available to the northern Ontario line if and when the Great Lakes project materializes. Idle capacity would then be available for additional sales of interruptible gas if required by industry in northern Ontario. I have already stated that the assurance has been given that no "firm" gas had been refused to industry in the area. What may have been refused is interruptible gas.
My reasoning is simple. If there is a second line, more space will, of course, be available in the northern Ontario line and consequently more gas will be provided for people served by it.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Therefore, I really do not understand exactly why the commission complains. It may complain because northern Ontario did not get the pipe line. My answer to that is; I am very sorry but circumstances do not permit. We have tried, however, to safeguard this advantage for 1970. I think this is a defenda-ble compromise. With respect to the availability of gas in northern Ontario the assurance is given. It seems to me to be a fact that if we have two lines there will be more room in the northern Ontario line for gas going to industry in that area.
The brief talks about the great potential mine development in the Pre-cambrian shield, and just a little while ago the hon. member for Nickel Belt referred to this. It is the responsibility of the National Energy Board to make sure that gas is first made available to Canadians, and it fulfils this responsibility. It would be quite difficult to justify the building of a pipe line solely on future prospects. The gentlemen who are willing to pay the cost of pipe lines usually like to work on something more concrete than potential developments. Therefore if northern Ontario should grow and grow, and become the richest part of North America, something which I hope very much will happen, there is no doubt that further looping will take place. But in the meantime, it does not seem justifiable to build a pipe line on future prospects.
May I also say that gas will be provided by the Great Lakes line to Sault Ste. Marie at a reasonable cost, and that the use of the Dawn storage fields for the moving of gas in and out of storage will benefit customers, because of the lower transportations costs.

Another advantage is that the Great Lakes project promoters have contracts with the distributors already signed.
It has cost the company quite an amount of money to do all the necessary preparatory work. If we were now to kill this project, we would destroy the preparation of months and years, the company would have to renegotiate a different project, which would be quite expensive.
There are many more points I would like to cover, but I shall deal with only one more. Some hon. members seemed to be flabbergasted by the fact that the 30 inch pipe line in northern Ontario will be carrying more gas than the proposed 36 inch pipe line through the United States. The answer is that it is not a question of diameter but of volume. I am no expert in these matters but volume is conditioned by pressure, by the number of compressors which are put on a line. You can get more delivery by adding more compressors.
May I also point out that there could be a quantity of gas for export going through the Great Lakes line. When you assess the capacity of the Great Lakes transmitting line you must deduct the amount of exportable gas going through it. This will be quite a good percentage. I cannot say precisely what this percentage will be because this, of course, will depend on sales made in the United States and these have to be approved by the National Energy Board.
Is it not true that at least one third of the gas going through the Great Lakes line will have to be exported in order to keep within the terms of the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I can only say that this is a reasonable possibility.
In conclusion, the declaration that more than 50 per cent will go through the northern Ontario line is not an absurdity. The looping of the northern Ontario line will begin in 1970, and at all times more than 50 per cent will be carried by the northern route. By 1976 more than 60 per cent, and within a further reasonable period of time 65 per cent of the gas will be carried. All of this is a very rational prospect.
That is the story, Mr. Chairman. These things must be considered with reason and in a peaceful atmosphere. I am not one to say that the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines project is the absolute in perfection. I can only say that it is a good project in the present circumstances. The producers in western Canada
November 1, 1966

will be given the opportunity to produce more gas. Apparently these gentlemen are very aggressive in their efforts to produce more gas, something which applies to oil producers as well.
There will be more production of gas and industries in eastern Canada want more gas. We had representations from the presidents of consumer companies begging us to go ahead with this project because they needed the gas. Now, if this project is accepted by the United .States Federal Power Commission they are going to have their gas. At the same time we feel that we have protected a future advantage by ensuring that the northern line will be looped beginning in 1970.
Some hon. members may ask what about control by the United States Federal Power Commission? I am not going to say that this is not a problem, but by making sure that the main line will be in Canada, I think we have minimized the possible disadvantages of the control that the federal power commission would have on this line.
Hon. members can say everything they want on this subject. They can pinpoint disadvantages here and disadvantages there. I will not complain. I might even at times agree, but I simply say that when you make a decision of this kind you have to line up the advantages on one side and the disadvantages on the other. This is what we have done and, taking into consideration all possible circumstances, we have decided that this project is more advantageous, despite any of the real or exaggerated disadvantages which hon. members have mentioned yesterday and today.

The minister has outlined what he thinks are the advantages, and I agree with him that there are advantages and disadvantages. It is a matter of opinion what the decision should be, on balance. But I want to ask him, did not all these advantages obtain when the cabinet rejected this proposal on August 25? According to the Prime Minister the cabinet decided that this should be an all Canadian project, and that the pipe line should be wholly and exclusively within Canadian jurisdiction. What happened to bring about this change of principle since the government decision of August 25?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I am frantically looking for my communique of August 25.
Read the last paragraph.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I shall:
This has been a difficult decision in a very complex matter. However, the gas transmission industry
Interim Supply
is a public utility on a vast scale, and is important to Canadian national well-being. The development of its main links between west and east should, we believe, remain wholly under Canadian jurisdiction.
This is what we have done. The hon. member can read as well as I do, and probably better, at least in English. It says that we believe; "its main links between west and east should remain wholly under Canadian jurisdiction". That is very clearly what has been ensured, and I do not feel there is any contradiction.

But the government rejected the proposal at that time. If the minister will read the Prime Minister's statement, he will see that the Prime Minister said the cabinet had rejected this because we would lose control of the operation and this could cause embarrassment with the United States government.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Because we lost control of the main link between western and eastern Canada? You will have to look quite a long time, I think for many years, to find a contradiction in the communique. From the beginning, the decision was to keep the main line in Canada. As I said before to the hon. member, I think we made only one decision. The idea of saying the government has revised its decision, in my view, is quite wrong. I explained that to some people in Calgary who now see the light. Some of them said they regretted not having seen it before. I think the hon. member will do the same thing, in due course.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. My remarks on interim supply will be in connection with the Department of National Defence. Because of the minister's evasive action, I think the Canadian public is becoming concerned and alarmed that all is not well within the Department of National Defence. The Canadian public is becoming suspicious that the minister is attempting to bring about an ill advised, radical change in the policy we have been carrying out in the past, a change which would be contrary to those policies which have proven themselves. In fact, I think the minister, by his remarks in the house in the last couple of days, and by his press releases, has conveyed to the public of Canada an impression that there is some mystery behind what is taking place in his department at the present time.

November 1, 1966
Interim Supply
I wish to say also that the minister is adding to the suspicion by his reluctance to give intelligent answers to questions asked by responsible members in this house. Reference has been made this afternoon to a great number of those questions by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. Hon. members have related that they are not satisfied with the answers the minister has given. Last week, when the minister was asked a question about a reduction in the armed services of 23,000 personnel, he replied that he had saved the country $150 million. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre later asked him why he did not forecast a similar reduction for next year, and save another $150 million.
It gets increasingly difficult.

pass rapidly and efficiently to a war footing. This always has been the policy in the past, and I think it should be the policy in the future. If our military structure is not capable of assuming the burden which will be placed on it in the event of the requirement to mobilize our military force to maximum national capacity, then I think the minister will agree that it is of doubtful value. He might as well tell us all the facts, and save the Canadian people the money they are spending for defence today.
Common sense tells us the technique of war is rapidly changing, and all nations must adjust their thinking to cope with these changes. Canada is no exception. However, only under a dictatorship can a radical transformation take place without questions being asked by the public. In a democracy it is not enough to trust blindly to the government to take wise decisions on these vital matters. Every responsible citizen has a duty to understand for himself, as the minister said, what is happening, and to exercise his judgment even on questions as difficult and complicated as integration and unification in our armed services. The disadvantages, it seems, have been completely ignored by the present minister. There are many reasons such a move may prove to be a very dangerous military experiment. I believe this is what the minister is doing; he is carrying out a very dangerous experiment. The Canadian public now is asking why the minister, at this time, decided to make this experiment, particularly when all other miiltary powers, after investigation, decided against it.
The minister has said in press releases that other countries will follow suit. I should like to ask the minister what he means by saying "other countries will follow". Some suggestion has been made that it might be Sweden or Switzerland. As the minister knows, both these countries are neutral countries.
Tell us about the Swiss navy?

He will come to that later. My concern on this issue is, why has the Minister of National Defence chosen to ignore the advice of his top military advisors and arranged for their retirement from their respective services?
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Surely, the issue is not as the minister stated in mid-July in Edmonton, "civilian control over the military". I think the minister owes this house an explanation of that
Interim Supply
statement if, in fact, he made it to the press. What is this controversy in respect of civilian control over the military? I, for one, certainly do not believe for one moment that any of our senior service personnel were planning a coup, and if that is what the controversy is about the minister owes it to the people of this country and this House of Commons to say so. What is behind all this except political expediency? I refer to this statement about civilian control over the military. There has never been any question in Canada about the military taking control of civilian authorities. Thinking Canadians are not gullible enough to accept that kind of statement.
Canadians realize that the adviser's role is to provide facts and figures, as well as warnings of any risks involved. It is the duty of the minister's military advisers to point out the consequences of any unorthodox action he may be contemplating. It is my belief that the minister revealed what he was contemplating to some of these high ranking advisers, and I should like to know what he was contemplating. Parliament surely has a right to know the real cause of the controversy and the reason for the changing of 13 senior officers in the space of three months. The mystery created by what has happened in the minister's department has caused people to ask about these changes. As someone has said during this debate, the number of changes has increased from 13 to 40 senior officers.
Is the real cause of these dismissals related to the fact that advice given by senior officers proved to be right at the time the minister decided to discharge 500 newly trained jet pilots? The minister admitted in the house that he made a mistake which cost over $100 million. I hope he will compare that to the $150 million that he says he has saved because he has not been able to recruit replacements.

The previous government
wasted $100 million by training them in the first place.

I should like to know what happened in respect of these jet pilots. The minister has also said that we do not have enough technicians because no replacements have been trained for those who were discharged. In the face of this situation, many of our ships and aircraft are idle. As the junior member for Halifax pointed out last night, some of these ships are tied up to wharves in Halifax. What good is this equipment if we do not have the personnel and technicians to operate it? What good is the acquisition of more equipment if it cannot be used? Neither

November 1, 1366
Interim Supply
a cannon nor a rifle is of much use if it cannot be fired, and the same is true of ships and aircraft without personnel to operate them.
I should like to know whether the minister agrees with the statement of his present chief of staff who is reported as having said that the possibilities of total war are not considered great. If the minister does agree with that statement, how can he reconcile it with a recent statement by Reuters from Peking to the effect that:
China told its people yesterday to prepare for war sooner or later with the United States-perhaps within a year or two.
Would not such a statement lead the minister to believe that his present chief of staff is not facing up to the facts, and that Canada should consider the possibility of total war very great? Should Canada not be prepared to play its part in the defence of this continent, if and when that is necessary? This is one of the dangers I referred to when I spoke in this house at the time the defence committee was first formed. This same reference was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre.
Let me repeat what I said at that time on the subject of organization and senior personnel. I believe we have delegated too much power to the chief of our general staff. When the defence act was revised in 1950 personal authority was given to the C.G.S. far beyond that of his counterpart in the British army. British parliamentary reforms, established the principle that no single commander in chief should have sole responsibility for control and administration of the services. Since 1904, after the Esher reforms, the British army has been administered by an army council composed of political, military and civil service officials. The council has survived severe tests in two world wars, and has remained an effective and efficient instrument of government policy in the administration of the services.
The weakness of full military control similar to that in effect at present in Canada has been illustrated over and over again in other countries. I refer to the warning in Germany when their original idea that one man should have sole responsibility for all services was defeated.
One of the pitfalls resulting from the power Canada's parliament has delegated to its chief of staff is the natural tendency for anyone to gather around him like-thinking friends. In this regard, I think the minister dug very deeply into his resources of military advisers to get someone who would say yes to

every suggestion he made. I also said in 1963 that when everyone thinks alike, no one thinks at all. I believe that is what is happening at this time.
Only a Tory would know that.

You are not sorry that you do know that, surely.
There are many questions I should like to ask this minister. This minister has ignored the total weight of the professional opinion of all his senior advisers. He has disregarded the clear and repeated lessons of military history, and he has disregarded the practical knowledge and advice of top British, United States and Canadian commanders who have proven their ability in battle.
These are some of the questions I should like to ask the minister. Why has he disregarded the decision of military powers who have discarded the idea of unification? Has the minister and his government decided to adopt a policy of neutrality or isolationism for Canada? That is an important question in my mind. What purpose is to be served by disbanding our three military forces? I think the Canadian people are entitled to know the answer to that question. Is it the minister's intention to eventually withdraw our forces from military alliances such as NATO and NORAD? Is it the intention of the minister to leave the defence of Canada to the United States? Why has the minister decided to scuttle our armed forces? Surely, we are entitled to know his motives. I should like to know whether they have anything to do with ideas recently expressed by the author Terence Robertson or does he believe that NATO has outlived its usefulness and is now philosophized, as some writers put it?
I will admit that in the case of NATO and NORAD the principle of defence has changed and countries can no longer guard their borders as they did in days gone by, but does the minister believes that NORAD no longer needs Canadian participation? It is obvious that the concept of defence has changed completely so that we must now guard our borders on a continental basis. However, I think the pride of the Canadian people should be considered, and we should take our part in any future defence of the North American continent. I realize we have only one tenth of the power possessed by the United States, and I am sure that everyone in the house will agree that the United States intends to guard the North American continent whether Canada wants to be guarded or not. Most

Canadians do want to participate in that defence. Let us be proud of this part we play. Let us not divorce ourselves from this idea or remain smugly under the umbrella of United States defence of this continent, whether we like it or not.

I am quite convinced that the existence of NATO has prevented a third world war. In this connection, I ask the minister another question: Has he adopted this policy because he believes that only the United Nations remains as an inspiration for external defence policies? From time to time suggestions have been made that we should turn over part of our armed forces to the U.N. To date there has been no inclination on the part of the U.N. to accept this kind of offer-

-and, say projected to 1970, or is there going to be a short-fall in the commitment as now outlined?

We need one single armed service under one supreme Chief of Staff in one uniform. We need to organize our armed forces in the form of task forces designed for their particular jobs, at home or off our coasts or in Europe or with the United Nations. They would all come under one system of administration, and by this means-and only by this means-I believe, the taxpayers' legitimate complaints of extravagance, duplication and waste can be removed and Canada can start to get real value for its defence budget.

appeased, my mind put at rest when I saw a man with such experience, holding an absolutely necessary position, realize the urgent needs of the Canadian forces and come up with that advanced formula, as it were, of the problem which is facing us today. Mr. Chairman, we are blamed for our failure to consult high-ranking officers, but there is a national' defence forces council where they are grouped. For instance, we have seen recently the new armed forces pay structure. Mr. Chairman, I have been aware for two years that a large committee of experts is working on this complicated question of the army pay system. In that way, we arrive at a highly efficient system, and I do not see why, in a $1.5 billion enterprise, in Canada, we should be blamed for wanting to apply modern administrative and control methods.

I listened to the Associate Minister of National Defence make his eloquent and sincere remarks, but I believe he protesteth too much.
I think all members of the house will agree that the calibre of officer remaining in the Canadian forces is high, as this transfer to a hybrid force takes place. The trouble is that the Minister of National Defence and the associate minister have more facts and figures at their fingertips than other hon. members. Perhaps their confidence is justified. I intend, in my participation in this debate, to ask the Minister of National Defence to follow the admonition of the Prime Minister. Let the minister take his feet out of the bucket of sand. Let him revise his thinking, and hold defence committee hearings so that we can explore in detail all the ramifications of the integration-unification program.
The minister no doubt may be correct in what he says, when he refers to the white paper. The trouble is that when the white
November 1, 1966

paper came in, in 1964, many members presently in the house were unable to participate in the debate on it. Whether those members participate constructively or not, they at least ought to be given the chance of participating. At the moment, in the supply debate, there are many issues before the country, and many members on all sides of the house are sincerely concerned about where the integration-unification road is to end. If we had the benefit of some of the advice given to the minister and to the associate minister we might share some of their confidence. This may not be entirely possible, but the minister could at least convene the defence committee with the consequent hearing of witnesses. That would help.
If the minister believes that what is being done represents a step forward in defence, represents the great new politics and the great reasoned approach, why does he not go one step farther and convene this defence committee?
The Prime Minister gave words of advice which I am sure the minister would wish to heed. Those words of advice were given at a certain convention in June of this year, as reported in the Toronto Telegram of Thursday, October 13. The Prime Minister is reported to have said:
Remaining firm and immovable in a bucket of hardening cement is nothing to boast about. Political leadership is being steady not stuck.
There is a bucket over his head.

There is no bucket over anybody's head, but we want to see some cement on the other side of the house. Since parliament convened in January we have seen it bogged down in one kind of cement. In some ways, though, I think the minister is to be given credit for making advancements in a program which has new avenues to explore. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre reviewed the history and the halos surrounding some of the minister's statements. That review was in major tones. The hon. member for Calgary North pointed out the so-called savings and the so-called substitutions, again in reasoned tones. There are many across this country who want to develop and explore this topic of defence, but they want to do that in reasoned tones.
Knowing this requirement, with which all members agree, why does the minister not convene the defence committee? If the defence committee were convened we might question the witnesses, and gain some information.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Let us at least call the witnesses before the defence committee, then perhaps we can get on with this debate and proceed to other business which is also pressing. Frankly, I have real reservations about the value of unification and integration. The process did not start with the present minister, of course. In a sense, General Eisenhower and General Montgomery were commanders of integrated forces. The minister has taken pride in saying that Canada is a showcase for his policy. Of course, Canada is a showcase. This is a new program and all countries are interested in seeing how it is progressing. It is like watching micro-organisms on a slide; everyone is interested in looking through the microscope to find out whether they will live. But they do not want to get onto the slide themselves.
If the minister would agree to reconvene the committee and let witnesses be heard, he might be able to convince those countries abroad which are watching this experiment that unification will strengthen our armed forces, not emasculate them.
The minister has pointed with pride to the example of certain countries abroad. I intend to refer, not to Great Britain but to a country which is like Canada in many ways as far as the size of its population is concerned and the potential of its contribution to world order. I shall take the example of New Zealand, and place on record part of an article from the Canadian Press about the New Zealand white paper. New Zealand has studied the Canadian experiment and come out positively as saying that the type of force Canada is advocating is not a force which would be suitable for

New Zealand. I quote from a report which appeared in the Chronicle-Herald of June 11: A force of this type which New Zealand could afford to maintain in peacetime would never be large enough to give a truly independent role in limited war. Because of the 'separateness' of the three services of all our principal allies, a combined New Zealand force would have to be logistically self-contained or largely so. The government has concluded that New Zealand can make a larger, more flexible, and more effective contribution to collective defence and to the demands of the cold war in the form of three separate service elements than with a combined balanced 'national force'.
The white paper refers specifically to the study made in Canada, and suggests it is specious and foolish to think that we in Canada could ever have a truly independent striking force. We are simply not large enough. We have to integrate our own forces with those of other countries. We are not a military power, and we should not pretend we are. If the minister has clearly defined road signs indicating the end of the path along which his policy is leading, perhaps he will tell us about them. He might even obtain agreement in this house with the idea that we are supposed to become a peace-keeping nation. But let us call the committee, and let that committee have power to call witnesses.
I suggest that New Zealand has adopted a reasonable and logical approach to this question on the basis that New Zealand, with a population of about 2,500,000, will never be able to provide a truly independent mobile force which would mean anything in terms of international power. The same applies to Canada.
If the minister has something else in mind, and he thinks it is so good, why does he hesitate to convene the committee so that we can study his proposal and dissect it? Let him take his feet out of the barrel of cement. I could understand the minister standing firm in his purpose, but let him not stick obstinately to his refusal to convene a committee which could direct us out of this dilemma. The experts and the critics could be heard. Perhaps the hon. gentleman himself could find some answers which have not been given as completely as they should have been.
There is another element which causes me concern. I refer to the implications of this policy as far as the maritimes generally and my own constituency in particular are concerned. I would remind the minister that his counterpart below the border, Mr. McNamara, had his defence problems-and he blazed a lot of new trails. But he did not act specifically for his own purpose, and

refuse to act when others made their wishes known. When there were painful decisions to be made he had a computer make the plan, and he published the decisions right across the country so that everyone knew what the implementation of the policy would mean.
The base consolidation plan is not a new idea. This was started a long time ago by McNamara. I wish the minister would play "McNamara's Band" and let the people know what the implications of his policy are. The radar station is closing in Kamloops; the base at Cornwallis is to be closed. The minister is not showing us his whole hand. He shrugs off criticism from this side of the house; he cannot be too much concerned about the constructive criticism that comes from over here. Let the people have an idea of the full import of these plans. Perhaps they can somehow be persuaded to believe that the end result will be to the benefit of Canada. The withholding of information, and the confusion to which it leads, will never win the confidence of people who might very well be on the minister's side.
Not much public support is aroused by taking a stand behind a few Generals or a few Rear Admirals. But I think the opposition in this house has a real responsibility to try to find out what is happening to a quarter of our budget.
I thought that the minister, taking pride in the announcement he made last night, would have referred this whole matter to the defence committee, taken it out of this partisan area and discussed the subject with defence experts, his own men and interested bystanders present.
I suggest we have international integration right now. We have it in Cyprus, in the Gaza Strip and in Viet Nam. No countries other than the United States and the Soviet Union are in a position to have independent striking forces in today's world, and the sooner we face this fact the sooner we shall know where the minister is heading. If he has in mind a peace-keeping force for the United Nations, he should let us know about it. The mass of the Canadian people may well be on his side. But the present confusion, together with some flippant answers from the hon. gentleman, does nothing to win confidence from this side of the house, let alone from the people at large.
I think the people of Canada will be amazed when they realize the full import of this consolidation program.

['Mr. Speaker, yesterday I drew the attention of the Solicitor General of Canada to the fact that a poor little bunny girl and four stock traders had been charged in Toronto with operating a hockey and football lottery. The details available to us in Toronto simply are that they were printing tickets, one for each second of the hockey game, and selling these for $1 each. The person who had the proper second at which the winning goal was scored in the professional hockey game played in Toronto would come in for a small prize. I use the word "small" because of the comparison with the vast amount of money that would be secured by the sale of the tickets.
Evidently the government is enforcing the present pristine pure laws which we have against lotteries and sweepstakes in this country. It is interesting to know that they have even come down to the level of the poor bunny girls in taverns. I only hope that when they served the summonses on the four stock traders on the Toronto stock exchange those men were not selling Windfall stock at the time, because it would be a laugh to them to be served with a summons for selling lottery tickets when they might have been selling Windfall stock.
Having sympathy for the poor little bunny girl, I asked the Solicitor General if any action is being taken against the bank presidents of this country who are selling the premium savings bonds, series B, put out by the British government. I buy these right here in Canada, usually in Toronto, and have no trouble whatsoever. I hold in my hand a prospectus for these savings bonds. The British government calls them premium savings bonds, and I suppose the Canadian government recognizes them as premium savings bonds, but everybody else in this world knows them as the British lottery bonds.
November 1, 1966', 'These bonds were first discussed in 1956. You can read all the details in the British Hansard in the parliamentary library. The suggestion first was made by Lady Tweeds-muir, a member of the British House of Commons. She was the wife of the son of a former governor general of Canada. It is a terrible thing to think that the fact that her husband lived in Canada for four or five years and was exposed to the purifying atmosphere of our lottery laws had no influence on her introducing such a heinous thing as lottery bonds. But worse than that, Lady Tweedsmuir was supported in the introduction of these lottery bonds in the 1950's by the prime minister of Great Britain, Harold Macmillan, who spent five years in Canada. I regret that we had no influence on the lives of those people who had resided here. If people like Lady Tweedsmuir and Harold Macmillan can spend years in Canada and return to Great Britain still wanting to buy sweepstake tickets or, indeed, start a sweepstakes, I think we can realize why Canadian citizens who live in this country are interested in buying whatever sweepstake tickets are available.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
This British lottery bond institution is an amazing one. Every month it has a draw for prizes and you can get a prospectus from any Canadian bank. I have underlined on this prospectus a score of places referring to draws, prizes, drawings, monthly draws, monthly prizes, and the word "drawing" would indicate to anyone but the Canadian cabinet that these are lottery bonds.
Is the cabinet going to take any action against these bank presidents? I do not like to see the police instructed to confine their attention to tavern bunny girls and stock traders who are dealing in stocks that make lottery tickets look like a wisk of wind in a hurricane compared to what they are selling on the floor. I wish the police would spend some time in respect of these men who are dealing in lottery bonds.
Anyone can go to the banks and get a prospectus which sets out exactly what you must do. Of course the bank itself does not actually sell you the bond. The clerk tells you to go over to the foreign exchange counter where you buy a British pound note for every bond you want and you then mail the pound notes to Great Britain. This whole thing is conducted by the British government through the post office and there are two
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion addresses given: General Post Office, London,
E.C.l and Premium Savings Bond Office, Lytham St. Annes, Lancashire.
Is the Canadian government stopping all the mail going to the General Post Office, London, E.C.l and to the Premium Savings Bond Office, Lytham St. Annes, Lancashire, as it does in connection with Irish sweepstake mail? You cannot use the mail to sell Irish sweepstake tickets. This prospectus points out that the British government will inform the winners of monthly draws by post. Has the Canadian post office no instruction through the Solicitor General to examine mail coming into Canada by post from the British government?
It says in rule 10 on this prospectus that the winners will be notified by post. If the post office is going to stop the mail going to the Irish hospital sweepstakes because this transgresses the postal regulations of Canada, why does it not stop mail going to these addresses in Britain, because this also breaks the laws of this nation?
Far be it from me to ever suggest that the Canadian cabinet should adopt such a sensible idea as a lottery bond so that the people of this nation might have the opportunity of paying off the national debt in a manner that would appeal to many of them. As Mr. Harold Macmillan said in support of Lady Tweedsmuir: If the people are willing to forgo the certainty of interest in order to have a chance of winning a prize each month that is nobody's business but the buyer of the bond.
I cannot see any reason why Canadians should not be given the opportunity of buying Canadian lottery bonds put out by the Canadian government in the same way the British government puts them out, but until the cabinet wakes up and smartens up considerably and introduces such a sweepstake in Canada in order to reduce the Canadian national debt, I simply want to know whether they are going to enforce the law of the land only by chasing bunny girls through taverns and prosecuting stock traders while they flimflam the public on Bay street. Certainly the cabinet ought to prosecute these banks which are issuing the premium savings bonds prospectus, series B, and selling foreign exchange so you can send it to England and get your bonds back by post. Why should we just chase the little bunny girls and leave the bank presidents alone?
