speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Port Arthur.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday afternoon I was not aware that the very important subject of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines was about to be debated. As is quite proper I was attending to other responsibilities in the committee on transport and communications. It came to my attention after the dinner hour last evening that it was the subject of the discussion. In reading yesterday's Hansard with great interest I noted at page 9316 that the hon. member for Timmins had made reference to me in these words:
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
The other day the hon. member for Port Arthur read to the delegation from the north, before they met with cabinet members, a carefully prepared and very sound statement-
I feel quite sure that having brought this to his attention he will want the record to be corrected. He was present at that meeting and knows that my statement was made in the joint presence of cabinet members and the members of the delegation and not to the delegation before it met with cabinet members. As a matter of courtesy to the hon. member for Timmins I suggest that this error may have been one of transcription rather than any attempt to establish a significantly distorted history of this episode.
My stand on the pipe line has been quite well known since the Trans-Canada proposal was first made to the National Energy Board last December. With regard to the proposal which has been approved and was explained during the meeting to which I recently referred and on other occasions, my concern revolves around my conviction that the best interests of northern Ontario are not being met.
The deal now approved is unquestionably better than the first proposal by Trans-Canada which made no provision for expansion of the Canadian pipe line from Manitoba through northern Ontario. In terms of timing, however, the commencement of twinning the existing northern line in 1970 is not soon enough. I have asked as forcibly as I can that every attempt be made by the government to advance the commencement of the twinning and construction of the northern line, and I shall continue to press for such action.

We also want assurance that the existing price differential advantage between northwestern Ontario and eastern Canada is maintained when the economies of volume provide a price decrease, and we want that price decrease spread over the whole system. We would certainly be adamant about the benefits of that price reduction going to eastern Canada. The price advantage which exists now exists for good and sufficient reason, simply because we are closer to the source. In many other ways, however, we suffer disadvantage and discrimination. For example, in respect of freight rates we experience an unnaturally imposed disadvantage.
There is a third main consideration we in northern Ontario envisage. We want to see concrete measures taken as a matter of firm policy so that the supply of natural gas to our industries present and future will be a primary consideration before natural gas is exported as a result of this new plan.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is aware of the worry about the adequacy of natural gas supplies to northern Ontario industries, present and future. This worry has been expressed to him many times, most forcibly last Wednesday evening. On October 27, as recorded in Hansard at page 9167, the minister informed the house that one of his officials had telephoned a distributor in northwestern Ontario about the supply of natural gas and was told that the company has never had to refuse a supply of firm gas. He said that the problem lies with interruptible gas and that a pipe line could not function solely on the basis of an interruptible gas supply. The people in my constituency are asking, as I think they quite rightly should, for a more complete investigation of the question of gas supply. On that aspect I have what I think is a concrete suggestion for the minister.
I specifically ask that the National Energy Board delegate to at least one of its senior members the responsibility of accompanying the minister, myself and other interested members from northwestern Ontario to that region to check at first hand the present and future needs of that area. If this can be arranged I will schedule meetings with industrial consumers, not just distributors, throughout that area. I most certainly will include in that tour a visit to the iron ore centre of our area to see one of its representatives who only yesterday informed me that the iron ore pelletizing potential volume in
November 1, 1966

our area is 18 million tons per year. At the present time production capacity is about three million tons so it can be seen that a significant increase can be forecast over the next few years.
Just to indicate the market trend in potential capacity let me refer to another example. One Canadian steel company recently indicated that its requirements would increase from the present level of one million tons of iron ore pellets per year to three million tons by 1970. While the 18 million pellet tons forecast for production in northwestern Ontario is unlikely to be on stream at one time it does not take sophisticated arithmetic to realize that natural gas requirements for that industry alone in that area alone are going to increase to billions of cubic feet annually. I give this as one example of information which may not be available or known to the minister or the National Energy Board. This is the sort of information that should be made available. I want to be assured, as do my constituents and others in northern Ontario, that factors of this kind are known as a result of first hand, on the ground investigations and that they are given proper consideration.
My own experience on the transport committee has proven to me that one cannot hold all hearings effectively in Ottawa, particularly on such a vital and contentious matter, and get the full story. This applies also to the National Energy Board.
I repeat, therefore, to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources my invitation to him and a senior member of the National Energy Board to accompany me and other interested members of parliament immediately on a field trip throughout northwestern Ontario.
Many facts have been stated for and against the pipe line decision, and in respect of my own area of northwestern Ontario I want to add an additional consideration. The pipe line, over and above its specifics, is really a manifestation of an issue on which has been based the frustrations of the people of northwestern Ontario. This situation has been developing for a long time as a result of attitudes on the part of both the federal and provincial levels of government. My colleague who represents Kenora-Rainy River expressed it most effectively last night and I am simply joining in his statement.
Northwestern Ontario is what I might call the unnecessarily underdeveloped heartland of Canada. It lies right at the geographic 23033-595
Interim Supply
centre of Canada and right in the centre of our distribution system. It is an area that has natural resources.
We in Canada know that we have a geographical distribution system which is uneconomic. One reason is the scanty population. Northwestern Ontario is about 250,000 square miles in area and has a population density 100 years after confederation of less than one person per square mile. These facts cause a real distribution problem and its effect on east-west trade is evident in many ways, not the least of which is the railway bridge subsidy which has existed for some years and is now going to be removed if the transportation bill goes through. In the interests of Canada I do not think it can be disputed that to realize the potential of the area it should be developed, populated and industrialized. The economic facts and figures in respect of the population situation are an issue in northwestern Ontario, and I want to register this point with the government.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
Northwestern Ontario feels that it has been by-passed. It has suffered from a lack of designation. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has given hon. members a further example of what has happened in this regard. An industry that we were endeavouring to have come to our area decided to go to the Georgian Bay area near French River because of the designated area there and the lack of such designation at the Canadian lakehead. This is just another example of the apparent neglect of the federal government and provincial governments which has stirred the people in the area to feel very strongly that somebody must speak for them and work in their interests. If I do nothing more than register the fact that this feeling exists because of the actions of the government on this issue, there will have been some value in my remarks.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I wish to say that I want no part of the accusations of insincerity or other ulterior motives that have been bandied about and applied to the ministers who are responsible for the pipe line decision. I genuinely disagree with some of the factors and points leading to that decision and some of the results therefrom; but I have no hesitation in commending the ministers' sincerity in the taking of those decisions. I feel that the ministers concerned are overlooking the interests of my area and that in the broadest sense the interests of my area

November 1, 1986
Interim Supply
have to be recognized as being in the national interest as well. I also believe that even at this late date, the agreement between Trans-Canada Pipe Lines and the government having been tabled, major improvements can be effected in this transaction. I am quite sure this can be done, and I ask the government to pay great attention to the requests that have been put forward and do something to improve the pipe line arrangements.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks this evening will be related, as have been the remarks of most of my colleagues, to the question of defence and foreign policy. I thought I had better make this clear because my initial observations will be directed to some of the new rules changes in the house as they relate to this particular problem.
Last evening the hon. member for Peace River pointed out in great detail and very capably that a recent decision of the Minister of National Defence-the minister elaborated further in this regard-has done a great deal to damage and in fact destroy the new committee system that was established on a trial basis by the house. As you may recall, Mr. Chairman, a year ago, as a result of much criticism in the press and other public media involving dissatisfaction on the part of members of the house and the public generally, attempts were made to streamline and revise the rules of the house to try to bring them more into line with modem conditions.
As we are all aware, at the present time we are using the new rules on a trial basis. It was hoped by many that the new system of parliamentary committees would be a useful and effective means of providing information to members of the house and the public at large with regard to details of many of the complex problems that all Canadians face. The committee system has not worked out as well as was expected. I think we all realize this. One problem, of course, has been that the government has attempted to control all the committees. I might add that this is normal; it has always been the custom. But the government, having only 130 members, 25 of whom are members of the cabinet and thus not able to attend these committees, finds itself in a very awkward position in trying to maintain a majority in committees when several are meeting at the same time.
As a result we have found that in most of the committees it has been very difficult to obtain a quorum, and very often government members have been at fault in this respect. This is no fault of theirs, necessarily. It

simply stems from the fact that there are not enough bodies to go around when several committees are meeting at the same time. That is one mechanical fault.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Even a Liberal cannot be in two places at the same time.

I must say that my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre has made a very appropriate observation and I am inclined to agree with it. Another problem that has arisen in this regard is that apparently the government now has cold feet in connection with the activities of committees. Having the honour to be vice-chairman of the committee on external affairs, I know that a number of the members of that committee had great hopes for the committee system quite apart from examining the estimates in detail. In this regard the committee on external affairs has done very well. We spent a great deal of time on examining the estimates of the department and generally, I think, fulfilled our duties very well in this area. However, many of the members of that committee, which is rather analogous to the defence committee, hoped that when we had approved the estimates and sent them back to the house we might be given the opportunity of visiting the General Assembly of the United Nations for perhaps a week. We hoped that we might be able to discuss further such matters as Viet Nam, Rhodesia, NATO and other areas that are very important indeed and of great public interest in this country. But for some reason or other the government has not seen fit to do this. It has dragged its feet in this regard and has not seen fit to permit the committee to carry on in this way.
I now come to the defence committee. While I am not a member of that committee, it seems to me that the question of the integration and unification of our armed forces is a highly complex matter. This subject is very much misunderstood by almost everyone. It is a matter of great detail. Matters of this kind should be clarified because it is perhaps one of the most important subjects that will come before the house. As I understand it, the meetings of the defence committee have been frustrated by the government and, I take it, by the Minister of National Defence in particular.

He hasn't frustrated it; he just will not allow the committee to sit.
November I, 1966

I understand that the committee has not been permitted to sit, so it is unable to obtain information on this highly important matter. Some people might say that various parties in the house are playing politics on the matter of defence. I do not think that is the case. I believe that all members of the house of whatever party are very sincerely interested in the defence of this country and the policies to be applied in this regard. Our very existence may depend upon the policies the house decides upon.
Requests have been repeatedly made to the government to have this committee sit. I do not blame the minister entirely for refusing to allow the committee to sit, because his colleagues have supported him in this regard. I blame the government for this situation. Members of the opposition have repeatedly requested that the defence committee be called to sit in order that it may look very carefully into the questions of integration and unification, clarify the issues, call witnesses and hear what is going on so that when the defence bill is presented to the house, as the minister has assured us it will be, all hon. members and the public at large will be able to discuss this matter in an informed, intelligent way, which is not possible at the present time. I cannot understand why the government will not permit the committee to sit.
The decision of the government in this respect is inexplicable; there is just no reason for it. The only reason I can think of is that there are some aspects of integration and unification that the government fears will not meet with general public approval and for this reason it does not wish the committee to be called at this time. Therefore, when the bill reaches the house and receives approval in principle, which it no doubt will in view of the fact that the government has the largest group in the house and will probably be supported by some other group, the minister will be able to say: "Well, the bill has been approved in principle on second reading and anything the committee does does not matter." On a matter as important as this I believe the committee on defence should be called right away. Members of the house, the press and the public could then be informed of what is really going on with regard to the question of integration and unification. I do not know how we can discuss the matter when the bill reaches second reading and approval in principle if we are not apprised of a great many facts. I will deal with this point in a moment.
Interim Supply
There are a great many pieces of information to which we on the committee are entitled. First of all, there is the difference between integration and unification. It is generally understood that integration refers to the non-fighting branches of the armed services, that those associated with medical services, dental services, communications, supply, purchasing, accounting and the like should be amalgamated under one service instead of there being three.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
It is alleged that certain economies would result from this. I think most members of the house and most members of the public would agree with that. I understand, however, despite the fact that this step has already been taken, that to some degree costs have gone up rather than down. This is something we would like to know about.
The position with regard to unification is much less clear. The minister in his statements in the house and outside has never been very clear as to what is meant by unification, and certainly we do not know what the government means by it. It is generally understood that there is to be some sort of hybrid armed force, the members of which all wear the same uniform.
I recall that the minister told the house one day that there was no reason why a gunnery officer in the army could not replace a gunnery officer in the navy almost overnight. Perhaps the minister has forgotten that other duties besides gunnery are associated with these ranks. Certainly as an ex-naval officer myself I find it difficult to envisage such a situation. However, the question should be cleared up.
Are we going to have some jack-of-all-trades armed force? In these days of modern weapons and the high degree of specialization that is required to utilize modern military hardware, as it is often called, it would be very unusual indeed for a person not to be required to possess some specialty knowledge, as is the case in the army, navy or air force. These are all things that we should be informed about.
We have also been told that money is being saved by this change. I have been told that at Camp Borden and at many other camps in the country there are thousands of motor vehicles-trucks, jeeps, cars and the like- which have been parked for two or three years without turning a wheel, and this because of the restriction placed upon militia training. The minister should give us some

November 1, 1963
Interim Supply
information on this, or if not the minister those in his department. If these vehicles are not going to be used and are just gathering dust and deteriorating, they should be disposed of.
Another question to which we should like an answer is: Who is the author of the unification plan? It is apparent that no other military power, certainly no major military power such as the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, France, Japan or Germany, is attempting to take this step. It is obvious that many senior officers do not agree with the minister's plan. In fact, over 40 of them from all three services have retired or have been fired. That is why we would like to know who is the author of the plan.
The minister has stated that the heads of the armed forces are subject to the control of the civilian authorities, and with that we agree. Is it the cabinet that devised this new scheme? With the exception of the Minister of Industry, who has had some previous experience at a senior military level, no other member of the cabinet has had any military experience of any consequence. Who devised the plan and what is the competency of the person or people who devised it? We should be given the answers to those questions.
There is also another matter in this regard that is rather offensive. Apparently the minister has a rather good public relations organization, and I do not blame him for that; but as a result of this, all of us have seen some of these cartoons which run down, disparage and make fun of our senior officers, or ex-senior officers, in the armed services. These cartoons describe them as "Colonel Blimps", "Old Fogeys", "incompetents" and the like. Most of these men, Mr. Chairman, are my age and I do not consider myself an old fogey. I think I am about the minister's age and I do not suppose he considers himself as in that category. These are people who have had experience with our NATO allies, the best kind of training, and are dedicated men in the public service; yet they are lampooned by a lot of it, I may use the vernacular, "kooks" in the press of this country who make fun of these people because they think it sells newspapers and is suitable to the minister and some of his colleagues. I say it is very unfair and most inappropriate.
If this committee were ever permitted to meet, one of the most important things its members would like to know concerns the question of where we are going and what is our defence policy. It has often been said-

and this perhaps is the most important thing of all-that the armed services are the strong arm of the foreign policy of the government, and with that I agree. It has been said in this house on other occasions that defence policy should be closely integrated with foreign policy, and with that I certainly agree. There is no point in having military forces and appropriate hardware for them unless there is co-ordination with the government's foreign policy.
I should like to know what our foreign policy is. It is certainly hard to figure it out. What is our foreign policy, for instance, with regard to NATO? The government pays lip service to NATO and to its commitments to NATO. On the other hand, there is every indication that the government seems to have the intention of withdrawing from NATO, if not immediately at least at the first reasonable opportunity in the future.

On that point, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member will allow me, I cannot permit his statement to go unchallenged. This question has been raised in the house several times recently and it has been flatly denied by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I would not want the press or anybody else to pick it up as having any substance at all because it was not challenged.

I am very glad to hear the minister make that statement. At least we have had a definite answer to one question. I sincerely hope he is correct, but the indications have been otherwise. This is the reason we want this committee to reconvene, so that it can be given some information. I am glad the minister has said that. We have been able to obtain something this evening.
What is our policy with respect, say, to the recognition of red China? The Secretary of State for External Affairs, who I am sorry is not in the house at the moment, has been very evasive when questioned on that subject both inside and outside the house. It is a sort of "recognition if necessary, but not necessarily recognition."
With regard to the admission of the People's Republic of China to the United Nations the Secretary of State for External Affairs strongly advocates at the United Nations on behalf of Canada that it is necessary that the People's Republic of China be seated. When he was asked in the house whether we are
November 1, 1966

going to support their being seated, the minister said no. It is like the old saying:
Mother may I go out to swim?
Yes, my darling daughter.
Hang your clothes on a hickory limb,
But don't go near the water.
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
That is about the way we ought to describe our policy with respect to the admission of red China to the United Nations.
What is our policy, for instance, with regard to the Organization of American States? The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that he thinks it is a good idea. He personally is in favour of it, but his colleagues are not. What is our position there?
What about Viet Nam? We have given lip service to supporting the United States, but at the same time the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister have been making speeches in Canada and the United States criticizing United States policy with respect to Viet Nam. It is quite understandable that some of us are at sea as to what is the foreign policy of this country. We should also like to know what the policy with respect to our armed services is to be. How can we know what our policy toward the services should be if we do not know our foreign policy?
For some time it has been said-it was said by previous administrations, both Liberal and Conservative-that the United Nations is one of the cornerstones of our foreign policy. I certainly agree that it is. I believe that successive governments have regarded the United Nations as one of the cornerstones of our foreign policy, along with our support of NATO, the Commonwealth, and our special relationship with the United States. Perhaps the minister would avail himself of the opportunity to give us further information at this time about our forces. Perhaps we could hear about it in the committee. We want to know what will be the role of the new hybrid force that is being created. We can only draw certain conclusions so far. All of us in the house, I think, fully support Canada's role in the United Nations. Canada has been the key contributor to peacekeeping forces over the years. That policy has been continued by successive governments, and I do not think many Canadians, if any, would disagree with it. If there are any who do disagree, they can only be a very small percentage of the people. I want to make it clear that I entirely support this policy. But providing a specially trained force for this purpose and training all
Interim Supply
your armed forces only for this purpose are two totally different things.
I should like to commend the Secretary of State for External Affairs for his work with the United Nations. The idea of a specially trained force for peacekeeping operations at the instant requirement of the Secretary General when necessary, initiated by Hon. Howard Green when he was secretary of state for external affairs and pursued very strongly by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, is a very good one. I believe we are all glad to see the role that Canada is playing in various parts of the world in this regard. The indications are, and this is a question that the government should clarify, that our present armed forces policy is to make all our armed services into a sort of hybrid force which would be available to the Secretary General.
It is very hard to keep secrets on Parliament Hill, as those of us who have been here for some time know. Certainly there are stories from reliable sources to the effect that in a year or two-this has been mentioned by other speakers in this debate and I ask the minister to clarify the situation-or possibly longer, possibly in five years, the navy and the air force will be relegated to a purely transport role in this new hybrid force. If this is so it seems that we are putting all our eggs in one basket. That may be all right if we are aiming for some kind of hybrid force which will be available whenever the Secretary General may require it for peacekeeping operations under the auspices of the United Nations. I have already said, and I think most but not all members of the house would agree, that Canada should provide a specially trained force which will be a sort of police force to serve the United Nations. But there are many of us who do not agree with the proposition that all our armed forces should be put, like eggs, into this one basket. This is something that I think the minister ought to clarify for us.
If this is the case, what are our responsibilities toward NATO? The minister has told us that there is no intention of giving up our commitments to NATO. How would some hybrid, quasi-police force fit in with our NATO commitments? How would it fit in with our NORAD commitments, our commitments to the defence of North America? These things should be clarified for us. It is most essential that all of us should know about these matters. There have been rumours and we have heard stories to the effect

November 1, 1966
Interim Supply
that there are United States vessels in large numbers at our bases on the west coast. I was informed of this by another member of the house. It may be coincidental but it arouses a certain concern because of the unclearness of the government's policy in this regard.
We have heard from the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and other members that our naval forces have been greatly reduced. According to the evidence of Admiral Landymore-the expurgated evidence-we may have a great shortage of naval personnel and ships by the spring of next year. It may well be that it is the government's intention to put all our eggs in the United Nations basket and to provide forces for use by the United Nations. If that is the government's policy, I do not agree with it. On the other hand, if this is not the case and we are not able to carry our load in our commitments for North American defence or anything else, though this policy may save the taxpayers some money I have the gravest doubts about our independence in the future.
It is often said that our voice in Washington is not all that strong at the present time. But how strong would it be in the future if we had no forces to contribute to North American defence? These are things that are very much in the minds of the people, members of this house and the press. I cannot understand why the minister will not permit the defence committee to be called so that these matters can be clarified. Or why will he not clarify them himself? I hope he will clarify these things before the debate is finished. If he is able to, that will be fine. It would clear up a great many questions which have been worrying us.
In conclusion I revert to my first remarks which had to do with the committees of the house. I agree that perhaps on matters of policy members of departments should not be permitted to come before parliamentary committees and give evidence. Perhaps the minister in his remarks last evening may have had a point. But certainly there is no reason why senior members of departments or of the armed forces cannot give factual information to the defence committee and other committees of the house. If, as the minister says, senior civil servants and members of the armed forces cannot give evidence before committees, there is no point in these committees meeting at all because their purpose, as I understand it, is so that members of the house can become informed and can

better debate matters of importance in the house.
If the government accepts the proposition outlined by the minister last evening there is no point in these parliamentary committees meeting, and I would think that members of this house, particularly members of the opposition parties, should give serious consideration to whether they should attend such committees if they are not to be permitted to receive factual evidence. Certain classified material and other matters involving policy ought to remain the responsibility-

Would the hon. member
permit a question?
Certainly.
Has the hon. member read every bit of evidence that was presented to the committee on defence this spring by all the witnesses who appeared there?

I have not, but I do not see that that question by the minister is in any way relevant.
[DOT] (7:50 p.m.)
It was intended to improve the quality of debate. I do not know how anyone can say it is unsuccessful unless he took the opportunity to read it.

The minister can go on dragging in herrings, red, blue, or any other colour, but the fact is he did not permit Admiral Landymore to give certain evidence to the defence committee. The minister has expressed his views, backed up by quotations from the Ottawa Citizen, a journal which supports the government on every possible occasion. He has given his opinion and he is entitled to it. I do not agree with him. If the minister and his colleagues on the treasury benches take the same view, that not only facets but opinions should be withheld from parliamentary committees, there is no point in our having any committees or in anyone attending them. I hope this will be cleared up in the course of the present debate. The question was dealt with most effectively by my hon. friend from Peace River and I do not wish to waste the time of the committee by further argument. In any case I see that my time has expired and that I must resume my seat.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased that the hon. member for Oxford referred in the course of his remarks to the usefulness
November 1, 1966

or otherwise of parliamentary committees. I believe this is one of the matters which is worthy of serious consideration as this resolution is discussed.
It appears to me that in 1963 there was a strong movement for reform in parliament resulting in the establishment of a special committee on defence under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine and the vice chairmanship of the hon. member for Edmonton West. This special committee was truly representative of the House of Commons of that day-I believe this is consistent with some of the best scholarly criticism available on the work of parliament. I should like to refer hon. members to the words of Hon. John Bracken, for whom we all have great respect. During the debate on the speech from the throne in 1946 he said in part:
It is my view that the whole committee structure of the house should be revamped, many of the present committees having no relationship to reality and some of them seldom functioning. There should be ten or more committees to cover the work of the different departments of the government.
Doctor J. A. Corry of Queen's University made a similar proposal in 1954. This can be studied in the Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science, Volume 20, 1954, in an article called "Adaptation of Parliamentary Processes to the Modern State." He entertained the hope that members might become semi-expert in the field of work of their committees. This, I think, is in line with the recommendations of Professor Bernard Crich who wrote a book called "The Reform of Parliament", published in London in 1964, very much to the same point.
Before discussing the specifics of this Landymore case I should like to inquire briefly into the background of parliamentary procedure prior to the establishment of the special committee on defence. I would ask any serious student of the subject to look at the Hansard of March 19 and March 20 of 1962. In 1962 the Conservatives polled 37 per cent of the votes and elected 44 per cent of the House of Commons. They formed the government. I would ask any person who wants to be fair on this matter to study the quality of the answers which were given to questions on supply in connection with national defence during that period. I refer particularly to those two dates, March 19 and March 20. I took part in the debate at that time and I felt completely frustrated. It seemed we were given no indication at all as
Interim Supply
to the purpose of our armed forces or the direction of defence policy. We were unable to clarify the situation in regard to differences of view within the cabinet. More important still, we did not know where Canada stood on urgent defence matters.
I think it is not unfair to say that that administration failed and was in due course defeated on the basis of defence policy. And I think it is fair to say we learned far more from the associate minister of defence subsequently-I refer to what he wrote in his book "This Game of Politics"-than we ever did during the course of any discussion of the defence estimates in 1962.
Hon. Pierre Sevigny writes:
Certain members of the Tory government could not make up their minds concerning the exact nature of their duties. On the one hand, they knew that we had to face up to our obligation within the framework of NATO and NORAD, but they also feared the political consequences of arming our services with nuclear devices.
Later, he said:
There was a deep division between the pronuclear forces and those who wanted to change our military policies. These conflicting views could have remained a well-guarded secret for a very long time if the Cuban drama had not come along. But it did happen, and at this point the Tory machine started to fall apart.
A little later, Mr. Sevigny writes:
We were now in deep trouble, and though the energetic actions of President Kennedy eventually put an end to the Soviet's military plans in Cuba, few believed that Canada had played the part it should have during the desperate hours that preceded the enemy's withdrawal.
I well remember the meetings which were held at the time of that crisis in the office of the then leader of the opposition-meetings which the present Minister of National Defence and the present Minister of Industry and Defence Production attended. We were all seriously concerned about the difficulty experienced in our attempt to find out Canada's course in that grave emergency.
It is in the light of all these developments that the Minister of National Defence resolved that never again would our country go into an emergency so ill prepared with respect to basic defence considerations. I think it can be said he took a bold and courageous step in establishing a special committee on defence the vice chairman of which, by my nomination, was the hon. member for Edmonton West, and whereon the official opposition was generously represented.

Having read the foregoing I am immediately prompted to ask this question. Let me refer to a precis on unification that appeared in a Canadian army journal in 1958, written by W. H. Pope, MC, CD. In part he said:
It is the height of extravagance to have each armed service work independently-indeed, competitively. on its own pet projects.

Under unification ail the manpower in the force will be used to best advantage. No longer will the navy discharge men surplus when the army can't meet reinforcement quotas-the three services won't bid against each other on the open labour market.
He then said in summary:
A single unified service can fight any war better- even conventional war. In a nuclear war the disorganization caused by massive casualties will be such that chaos and defeat will ensue with anything less than a completely unified service.
Anybody who is interested in scholarly military writing on unification would I am sure also like to read what appeared in a Canadian army journal in 1959 in respect of problems of future war and the practical doctrine and organization required by land forces.

I have never heard anyone inside or outside this house suggest that the minister is such a military expert it would be wise for this country to act on his misguided military knowledge without the benefit of other advice. Certainly what we have seen happen causes us nervousness. Our entire argument is based on the suggestion made by the associate minister of defence that we must examine all the facts before coming to a logical conclusion.
Let me now say a few words about the speech of the hon. member for Leeds who appeared today to be somewhat befuddled. He engaged in a practice that is becoming all
Interim Supply
too frequent in this house, namely, an attempt to confuse the house and the public as to what actually has taken place. I do not like to be repetitious. However, when a member such as the hon. member for Leeds, who is a lawyer, gets up in the house and gives a version of the facts such as he gave I cannot accuse him of deliberately misleading the house, but I must come to the conclusion that he has not been able to understand what has occurred, has not been able to understand the facts of the situation or does not know them all.
In view of what the hon. member for Leeds has done, I feel it is my obvious duty to put the facts forward again as clearly and concisely as possible so that no one will be taken in by the sorry spectacle of a member who is supposed to be informed giving us such a lamentably twisted version of what the situation actually is. I am sure most members were in the house on Wednesday, October 12, when I made a formal charge. There is only one way such a charge can be made against another member. We have heard the challenge passed back and forth across the house on many occasions. An hon. member who wishes to make a formal charge must take full responsibility for his action. I did just that and these are my words to be found at page 8553 of Hansard:
My charge, Mr. Speaker, is simply this; that the Minister of National Defence has breached the privileges of this house by tampering with a witness in respect of the evidence to be given before a committee of this house, the witness being Rear Admiral W. M. Landymore, the committee being the standing committee on national defence, and the evidence in question being the admiral's brief presented to the committee on June 23, 1966.
The minister objected the other day to the fact that the notice of the charge arrived only a few minutes before he came into the house. That is true. But the important thing is that he had it in writing for consideration rather than merely having a verbal indication of it. It was in writing and he understood exactly what it was and that it was properly drafted.
Part of the difficulty arises from the fact that few members appreciate that all questions of privilege in this house have long ago been settled. There is no such thing as a new question of privilege. If one is to charge another member with a breach of privilege it must come within one of the established rules in the same way as a charge in a court of law. As a defence counsel, if my client is charged with an offence the first thing I do is look up the Criminal Code to see if the

November 1, 1968
Interim Supply
charge is spelled out in accordance with the Criminal Code. If it is not there is no such charge and obviously if there is no such charge my client cannot be convicted. It is, therefore, my duty to this house to make sure that the charge is spelled out, that it is one well recognized by this house, the British house and our parliamentary system through the years.
If my charge does not come within one of the established rules of privilege obviously there is no case and no charge. The minister referred to the use of the word "tamper" and alleged that I should have spelled that out. The essence of tampering with a witness is the improper method of dealing with that witness. Surely there is nothing more I can say to make that more clear. The essence of the charge is the improper handling of a witness. Obviously if a committee considered the charge and found that the minister had done nothing improper he would not be guilty of tampering. I can only clarify this by suggesting that it would be just as foolish to suggest that a charge of theft should allege improper stealing because, after all, the essence of stealing is the improper taking of somebody else's property. The charge of tampering is the improper method of dealing with a witness and the evidence he intends to give to the house. Perhaps I should read citation 308 in Beauchesne so that everyone will understand clearly what I am suggesting. It states:
To tamper with a witness in regard to the evidence to be given before either house or any committee of either house or to endeavour directly or indirectly, to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence is a breach of privilege.
That effectively sets out in essence what a breach of privilege is, and in order to be sure there was no misunderstanding I followed that wording in the formal charge I made.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
There was some suggestion that there was some difficulty with the word "tampering". In deciding what it means we have only to consider the fact that this word has been used for 100 years in this parliament and for more than 250 years in the British parliament. By this time there really should not be any doubt in parliament about what "tampering" means, because citation 308 continues:
A resolution to this effect was passed by the House of Commons on 21 February, 1700, and has been regularly renewed in every succeeding session, and in numerous instances persons have been punished for offences of this kind. Corruption or intimidation, though a usual, is not

an essential ingredient in this offence. It is equally a breach of privilege to attempt by persuation or solicitations of any kind to induce a witness not to attend, or to withhold evidence or to give false evidence. This matter was considered in 1935 by a committee of the Commons (United Kingdom) who reported that, in their opinion, it was a breach of privilege to give any advice to a witness which took the form of pressure or of interference with his freedom to form and express his own opinions honestly in the light of all the facts known to him, and the house resolved that it agreed with the committee in their report.
If I have clarified that situation so that even the hon. member for Leeds will understand it, I hope it will not be necessary to correct any other erring individuals in this regard, although I have found that some members of the press have had it explained to them in detail very carefully and have promptly gone out and distorted the facts again in such a way that I can only infer that they were not trying to be honest.
In the speech of the minister, since he has not taken the course of an inquiry which is the only way in which he can clear his name, he attempted today to put up the defence that of course he would have to put up if he appeared before the committee. He can correct me if I am wrong but his defence appears to be substantially this: The facts are not quite as I have presented them, there is a suggestion that the minister assumed Admiral Landymore had agreed and therefore this changed the situation, and the minister in his responsibility as minister had the right to do what he did.
I think we should deal first with the fact of Admiral Landymore's appearance. The minister has suggested that this service officer was appearing on the minister's behalf. Almost immediately Admiral Landymore took issue with that position. The witness was summoned by the defence committee. He therefore became a witness of the defence committee, no matter whom he was serving under. Whether he came from inside or outside the forces, whether he was a civil servant or a private individual, he was subject to the call of the house in the same way as witnesses are before the courts. His attendance can be compelled. He can be sworn. He can be treated, in other words, exactly as any other witness, and there is nothing in Beauchesne or any authority I have read on the subject which indicates that military witnesses are any different from any other witness called before a committee. The order that Admiral
November 1, 1966

Landymore obeyed in coming before the committee reads as follows:
1.	Standing committee on defence have asked for a briefing on organization and mission of maritime command at 0930, 23 June 1966 with preliminary briefing for minister at 0930, 21 June.
2.	Briefing to be unclassified between 45 and 60 minutes with 30 to 45 minutes for questions. Commander and briefing team are to be responsible for presentation and be prepared for questions.
There is no doubt about who is responsible for the preparation of the brief and who is supposed to be handling the questions, most of which the minister answered. Those were Admiral Landymore's orders. I continue:
3.	Briefing should include description of command mission, and brief review of organization. Present and projected savings in manpower and dollars should be included if reasonably firm. Description of equipment and command activities should be given. Mention should be made of Canadian forces bases consolidation as it affects command.
4.	Visual aids and other projections may be used. Charts, diagrams, photos of equipment should be produced on transparent slides for projection on rear projection screen.
That is the essence of the order that this witness received and which brought him before the committee as a committee witness not, as the minister has the temerity to suggest, as a representative of the minister.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would identify the document he was reading from?
This is a copy of a signal that 1 understand is the order requiring Admiral Landymore to appear before the committee.

Would the hon. gentleman table it or at least tell us its source, because I think he is giving the impression that it came from the committee rather than it being in fact a signal from the vice-chief of the defence staff? Also, Mr. Chairman, he might explain to the committee why Admiral Landymore ignored his orders in not submitting an unclassified brief, as was stated in the order.

I am not concerned about whether the admiral ignored his orders so much as I am about the fact that the minister overstepped his duty. I asked Admiral Landymore what his directions were and he gave me this copy of the signal. I have one quarrel with the facts that the minister sets out. I read from Hansard of yesterday, page 9347, 23033-596
Interim Supply
the top of the right-hand column. The minister was dealing with Admiral Landymore's testimony, or the brief with changes in it.
It was suggested that some extra copies of the unclassified portion of the brief might be made available. Subsequently members of the staff went over the brief in detail and suggested a number of changes including the rewriting of the section on personnel requirements and statistics. This section was sent to me to look at and following a quick reading at my desk in the House of Commons where it had been delivered to me, I noted that it was all right in so far as I was concerned, assuming the admiral was in agreement.
I read that far in the paragraph at the moment. I will now read from page 9336 of Hansard, the speech of the hon. member for Halifax in which he put on record the sworn affidavit of Admiral Landymore. In the left-hand column under paragraph 7 the following appears:
I attended the minister's office at approximately 9 a.m. June 23, 1966, prior to appearing before the standing committee that same morning.
He had appeared the day before with his brief and left it at the minister's office. This was the next step prior to appearing before the committee. The paragraph continues:
At the private meeting in his office, I was informed by the minister that the personnel section of my brief had been altered because he wished to have a more "positive" approach in personnel matters.
I suggest that perhaps the minister's memory is a little faulty in that apparently, according to his speech of yesterday, his recollection is that the brief was delivered to him at his desk in the house, whereas Admiral Landymore's sworn affidavit is that he appeared at the minister's office that morning before he went to the committee and it was the minister himself who informed him that the brief had been altered-
Mr. Chairman, that is not in the affidavit. Would the hon. member send me a copy of the affidavit? I am sure that is not in it because it is not in accordance with the facts.
I will be glad to do so.
Please do it forthwith.
I have not the affidavit here, Mr. Chairman. It is in Hansard.
You have distorted the record enough. Try to keep it straight.

Mr. Chairman, the minister is fond of making these statements. I have been

November 1, 1986
Interim Supply
reading very carefully from Hansard. Would the minister mind telling me where I have distorted the record so I can fix it up right now?
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Stick to the facts. That is what you were suggesting.

That is how much reliance we can place on the word of the minister. I have asked the question because I want the record to be accurate, but he persists in making these almost silly charges and then we see what they are.

The hon. member just said a minute ago that the admiral had been instructed by my office to change that section. That is not correct and he knows it. It is not in the affidavit. If it is, it is a lie.
No, he did not say that.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You are putting words into his mouth.
I suppose the minister has misunderstood me, so I will repeat what I said to make sure the record is clear.
You do not need to; it is already on the record.

I read from paragraph 7 of the affidavit, as recorded at page 9336 of Hansard, the left-hand column. The admiral said:
I attended the minister's office at approximately 9 a.m. June 23, 1966, prior to appearing before the standing committee that same morning. At the private meeting in his office, I was informed by the minister that the personnel section of my brief had been altered because he wished to have a more "positive" approach in personnel matters.
That is not true.

The minister has said that I have distorted the record enough. When I got up and read the statement as carefully as I could to make sure that I would be as factual as he has asked me to be, the minister attacked me and said that I had distorted the record. But he did not say how I was distorting the record. I would have thought he would jump to his feet and explain this apparent lapse of memory or this contradiction between his unsupported word and the sworn testimony of a very reliable naval officer as to what had occurred.
In most instances, Mr. Chairman, it would not be a critical matter whether the brief was
delivered to the minister in Ottawa or the minister informed the admiral in his office before he appeared before the committee that certain parts should be deleted. But if one looks at the defence that the minister is attempting to put forward to justify his actions in this regard, I think the matter is all-important.
From a reading of the statement that he made yesterday it appears that unknown to him some officials in his department had made some changes, that he had not bothered to look at them because they would not matter much and apparently Admiral Landymore would have agreed to them anyway. What a different story that is from the admiral having to appear in the minister's office and being told by the minister what the changes were, making it obvious to the admiral that the minister was taking the responsibility, that it was the minister's order, that the minister assumed authority to do this and therefore was effectively silencing the admiral.
In light of this, Mr. Chairman, does it not seem strange that so many members of this house should appear to be so puzzled by the apparent consent of or lack of complaint by the admiral? He is a man who has devoted many years of service to this country. His duties are deeply instilled and he deeply respects the tradition in the services that one obeys the minister. You must try not to embarrass him because it could embarrass him politically. Yours is not to reason these things; this is the responsibility of the minister.
I suggest that this correction of the record in connection with the manner in which these events actually occurred clears away some of the underbrush and not only brings home directly to the minister the responsibility for and the knowledge of what was done, with his admitting as much to Admiral Landymore, but it also removes any doubt as to the admiral's consent.
I would now like to deal with the question of consent. As was said by the hon. member for Greenwood in his very clear and lucid speech last night, consent would not really matter. I would go further, Mr. Chairman. In view of the clear cases on tampering with witnesses, if there was a conspiracy to prevent evidence being given to the committee on the part of the minister and Admiral Landymore the minister would still be guilty of a breach of the privileges of this house. He is tampering with the evidence that the admiral thought in his own mind was necessary

November 1, 1966	COMMONS DEBATES
to be given to the committee. That is the sum and substance of it.
Time is drawing to a close, Mr. Chairman, but I would dearly love to deal with the minister's idea of what the responsibility of a minister is. I am sure that when he referred to "Government of Canada" by Robert MacGregor Dawson, the only part that meant anything to him as he read it, and which is recorded at page 9346 of Hansard, the right-hand column, was the last sentence which reads:
-and he therefore has the power to overrule any of his civil servants at any time.
I imagine that the minister took those words very much to heart and that it was the only part of the quotation in which he was really interested. For my part, I thought it most significant that the first part of that quotation read in this way:
The minister can never afford to forget that he will be expected to defend and justify his department's policies before parliament and the country.
Of course, this minister is not very interested in that part of the paragraph. It simply spells out and reminds the minister that this is responsibile government. Responsible government means that a minister is supposed to be responsible to parliament.
There is a similar sort of extract on the same page, the left-hand column. You can see the graciousness and kindness of this minister, Mr. Chairman, as he hands out these little goodies to parliament. At one point in his speech he said:
I have therefore concurred from time to time in the appearance of military officers to make statements and to give testimony.
There is an implicit suggestion here, Mr. Chairman, that the witnesses do not appear because a committee summons them but appear through the kind offices of the Minister of National Defence who decides whether or not he will let them come. I suggest to the members of this committee that this attitude is one of those things that we have to look at very carefully and instruct the minister in very deeply before we are through with this affair. It is ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- MONTREAL-PROPOSED SITE FOR NEW HEADQUARTERS BUILDING
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- MONTREAL-PROPOSED SITE FOR NEW HEADQUARTERS BUILDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 7, 1966, as can be seen on page 8443 of Hansard, I put the following question to the hon. Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh):
Can the minister tell the house whether a contract authorizing the construction of a motel on the new C.B.C. site in Montreal has been signed and with whom?
More than a month ago, the people of Montreal and of the province of Quebec took alarm at the news that a motel comprising a few hundred rooms would be built on the C.B.C. site in Montreal. We have not been able until now to have exact information on such a project and I would appreciate it if the hon. minister or her parliamentary secretary would make a substantial statement tonight on that matter.
Among other things, we would like to know whether the decision was taken by the C.B.C., the federal government or the municipal authorities of Montreal, or whether it was sanctioned by the three authorities, or two of them?
The people of Montreal thought that the C.B.C. site would serve the entire purposes of that organization and provide for future extensions concerning radio and television.
November 1, 1966
9428	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
How is it that some authorities have accepted to hand over to business operation, irrelevant to the basic purposes of C.B.C., an important part of its site?
I would like the hon. minister or her parliamentary secretary to convince us that this hotel project will promote the purposes of the C.B.C.
As a second aspect of my question, I would like to know to whom the building contract and business operation has been granted? Many rumours are going about to the effect that a group of French Canadian financiers were interested in that project and were financially able to carry it out. However, it seems that their offer has not been taken into serious consideration and that a great opportunity was thrown away of encouraging French Canadians to promote an important project in the province of Quebec.
We understand that in business matters, the financial and administrative point of view is of prime importance, but financial resources and efficiency being equal, I cannot see how, in that great French city of Montreal, government authorities could show discrimination in favour of political friends or contributors.
That is the reason why, Mr. Speaker, I was expecting from the minister or her parliamentary secretary a clear answer on all aspects of the question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Bechard (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION- MONTREAL-PROPOSED SITE FOR NEW HEADQUARTERS BUILDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to thank the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), since he was kind enough to forward to the office of the Secretary of State this very afternoon, the text of the speech he just delivered.
The question raised more than a month ago, or about a month ago, by the hon. member for Sherbrooke, Mr. Speaker, fully shows the serious consequences of venturing into a question before scrutinizing all the facts, and also the serious result of causing public confusion, especially among the people of Montreal, who have been expecting for a long time the completion of this magnificent plan that is just taking shape, namely the Place des Ondes of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke asked the following question:
Can the minister tell the house whether a contract authorizing the construction of a motel on the new C.B.C. site in Montreal has been signed and with whom?


The answer to that, Mr. Speaker must be that no contract to build a motel has been granted to anybody by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on the site of the Place des Ondes in Montreal.
The truth about the whole matter is that the corporation-namely the C.B.C. and not the government, the two being entirely different entities-did not lease the Place des Ondes site, in Montreal, but part of the site to the Nami Investment Corporation for a motel construction project, which lease will in no way interfere with the Place des Ondes building project, in Montreal.
It is simply a lease granted to the Nami Investment Corporation by the C.B.C. for the eastern section, which is that part of the site eventually to be taken up as a parking area for the Place des Ondes or the C.B.C. in Montreal.
The Harvey Cagna & Halton Development Corporation granted its support to the promoters of the project, and the lease in question, since we must eliminate all doubts on the matter, is not for an indefinite length of time, but for a period of twelve months and one half, beginning December 1, 1966 and ending December 15, 1967. These are the facts concerning transactions between the C.B.C. and the Nami Investment Corporation with a view to providing shelter for people who will visit Expo, while Expo '67 is under way. Everyone knows that there is a shortage of accommodation, and visitors to Expo must be provided with shelter during that part of the year 1967, and I repeat that this in no way affects construction which has already begun at Place des Ondes; excavating operations, as the house undoubtedly knows, have been under way for some time.
Why was that contract refused to a group of French Canadian financiers in Montreal? Here again, the record should be put straight; that contract was not refused to a group of French Canadian financiers.
What happened is that a second proposal was made to the C.B.C. which, as I said, is not the Canadian government, and that proposal came after the first, after the Nami Investment Corporation had started negotiations with the C.B.C.
The terms were made by the C.B.C. and the officials of the Nami Investment Corporation were told: If you agree to those
November 1, 1966
terms, we are ready to negotiate with you. The second group, that is the French-Cana-dian group which came after, was told: We are ready to make the same arrangements with you, if the other group does not agree to the terms offered.
That, Mr. Speaker-to put the record straight here and to give the facts as they are-is what happened between the C.B.C. and the Nami Investment Corporation. And that project will not delay the construction of the Place des Ondes-

subtopic: TRANSPORT-TERMS OF REFERENCE OF ATLANTIC PROVINCES STUDY
speechtext:
As most members of the house know, Atlantic transportation problems are at present under special study and at some future time we can expect legislation pertaining to the recommendations. In 1926 the Duncan Royal Commission was set up to look into grievances of the maritime provinces and the letter I refer to was written by Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, dated Ottawa, April 17, 1926, and directed to the chairman and the members of that royal commission, I am glad to see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) in the chamber because he might be able to advise us whether other prime ministers in their time also wrote letters of advice to royal commissions. In this particular case the letter read:
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Gentlemen,-The government of Canada is asking you to undertake a task of national importance in inquiring into maritime province grievances. The scope of the inquiry is indicated by the Order in Council constituting the commission. My colleagues and I desire to emphasize our conviction that the commission should not interpret its instructions
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion or its duties in any narrow or technical sense, but should take every opportunity for the fullest and frankest discussion of the economic difficulties facing this part of the dominion, the endeavours which have been made to overcome them, the causes of any shortcoming in these endeavours, and the most effective and practicable remedies.
The question is not a new one. What is necessary now is to focus the discussion into a practicable program, to take stock of what has been done, of what has been left undone, and of what still may be done.
In carrying on your inquiries, I have no doubt that you will obtain much pertinent and helpful information from individuals and public bodies in the maritime provinces, and that you can count upon the full co-operation of the provincial governments. The federal government will have pleasure in placing at the commission's disposal the resources of its departments. The activities of the Departments of Agriculture, Marine and Fisheries, Railways and Canals, Public Works, Mines, Immigration, Labour, and Trade and Commerce, the Soldiers' Settlement Board, the Natural Resources Intelligence Service, as well as the Departments of Finance, Customs, and National Defence, have involved much consideration of maritime problems, and this information will be readily available. Perhaps particular use might be made of the staff and facilities of the Bureau of Statistics, which has available a wide range of data bearing upon practically all phases of maritime development and maritime relations.
I am sure that I am speaking for the people of Canada as a whole when I say that it is our earnest desire that the impartial and thorough inquiry which we anticipate will be made will result in clearing away any misunderstanding or lack of appreciation of one another's problems, and will assist in working out constructive policies for the continued development of the maritime provinces and the welfare of all parts of our common country.
With all good wishes,
I am yours, sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King
When I found this letter the other day, Mr. Speaker, I thought it was a heartwarming document, and because of the great interest in the maritime transportation study I thought it should be placed on Hansard of this particular parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: TRANSPORT-TERMS OF REFERENCE OF ATLANTIC PROVINCES STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we are indebted to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave) for reading this very interesting letter. I have in my hands the Order in Council setting up the Duncan commission, in light of the question which the hon. gentleman asked me the other day which was:
Are the terms of reference for the special Atlantic provinces transportation study as generous and specific as those given by the late Mr. King in the mid-20's to the Duncan Royal Commission?

9430	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I thought I might read first that excerpt from the Order in Council which deals with transportation. Just to have the continuity I think I should read from the beginning up to the end of that part of it:
The Committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated sixth April, 1926, from Right Honourable W. L. Mackenzie King, the Prime Minister, submitting that representations have from time to time been made on behalf of the people of the Maritime Provinces by resolution passed by the Legislature of Nova Scotia, by Boards of Trade and other public bodies and by their representatives in Parliament and the various legislatures, that the interests of the Maritime Provinces have suffered as a result of certain legislative and administrative measures adopted from time to time by the successive parliaments and governments of Canada. Such representations relate more particularly to the alleged failure to use Canadian ports for Canadian trade to the extent to which they might be utilized, and to the handicaps said to result from the operation of the schedules of rates chargeable for the carriage of goods on the railways uniting the maritime provinces with the other provinces of Canada and to the manner of administering that part of the Canadian National Railways system which was formerly known as the Intercolonial Railway by methods and conditions alleged to be inconsistent with the pledges given at the time of confederation in regard thereto and with the practice followed from the time of the construction of the railway until December, 1918.
I have read that because in answer to the original question which the hon. gentleman asked I want to point out that the Atlantic study on transportation-the word "Atlantic" rather than "maritime" is used because of the union of Newfoundland in 1949-is much broader that the Duncan study. That dealt with the use of the ports, and what was really meant was the use of the ports of Halifax and Saint John, and the rates charged on the railways.
Today we all recognize, important as the railways still are to the maritime provinces, that good road transportation, good air transportation, improved connections by sea between the various provinces, the causeway to Prince Edward Island, and the immense development that will be required in the huge hinterland of the Atlantic provinces and Labrador all call for a much broader study than anything contemplated in 1926.
It is true that one of the aspects of the study is a review of the Maritime Freight Rates Act which resulted from the Duncan commission. It is in no way contemplated that anything will be done to reduce the volume of support given to the region as a result of this legislation. What the study has

DEBATES	November 1, 1966
been asked to do is to see where that money has to be used in the most effective way in order to get the most effective results. But that is only one phase of this whole study which is the most comprehensive ever undertaken with regard to this matter. It is being supervised jointly by my department and the Atlantic Development Board. We hope to have the report of the study early in the year, perhaps by the end of March. Then it is hoped that it can be studied throughout the year 1967 with a view to having legislation in 1968. That is just a rough timetable.

subtopic: LOTTERIES-POSSIBILITY OF GOVERNMENT ACTION TO MEET INFRACTIONS
LOTTERIES-POSSIBILITY OF GOVERNMENT ACTION TO MEET INFRACTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I drew the attention of the Solicitor General of Canada to the fact that a poor little bunny girl and four stock traders had been charged in Toronto with operating a hockey and football lottery. The details available to us in Toronto simply are that they were printing tickets, one for each second of the hockey game, and selling these for $1 each. The person who had the proper second at which the winning goal was scored in the professional hockey game played in Toronto would come in for a small prize. I use the word "small" because of the comparison with the vast amount of money that would be secured by the sale of the tickets.
Evidently the government is enforcing the present pristine pure laws which we have against lotteries and sweepstakes in this country. It is interesting to know that they have even come down to the level of the poor bunny girls in taverns. I only hope that when they served the summonses on the four stock traders on the Toronto stock exchange those men were not selling Windfall stock at the time, because it would be a laugh to them to be served with a summons for selling lottery tickets when they might have been selling Windfall stock.
Having sympathy for the poor little bunny girl, I asked the Solicitor General if any action is being taken against the bank presidents of this country who are selling the premium savings bonds, series B, put out by the British government. I buy these right here in Canada, usually in Toronto, and have no trouble whatsoever. I hold in my hand a prospectus for these savings bonds. The British government calls them premium savings bonds, and I suppose the Canadian government recognizes them as premium savings bonds, but everybody else in this world knows them as the British lottery bonds.
November 1, 1966

These bonds were first discussed in 1956. You can read all the details in the British Hansard in the parliamentary library. The suggestion first was made by Lady Tweeds-muir, a member of the British House of Commons. She was the wife of the son of a former governor general of Canada. It is a terrible thing to think that the fact that her husband lived in Canada for four or five years and was exposed to the purifying atmosphere of our lottery laws had no influence on her introducing such a heinous thing as lottery bonds. But worse than that, Lady Tweedsmuir was supported in the introduction of these lottery bonds in the 1950's by the prime minister of Great Britain, Harold Macmillan, who spent five years in Canada. I regret that we had no influence on the lives of those people who had resided here. If people like Lady Tweedsmuir and Harold Macmillan can spend years in Canada and return to Great Britain still wanting to buy sweepstake tickets or, indeed, start a sweepstakes, I think we can realize why Canadian citizens who live in this country are interested in buying whatever sweepstake tickets are available.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
This British lottery bond institution is an amazing one. Every month it has a draw for prizes and you can get a prospectus from any Canadian bank. I have underlined on this prospectus a score of places referring to draws, prizes, drawings, monthly draws, monthly prizes, and the word "drawing" would indicate to anyone but the Canadian cabinet that these are lottery bonds.
Is the cabinet going to take any action against these bank presidents? I do not like to see the police instructed to confine their attention to tavern bunny girls and stock traders who are dealing in stocks that make lottery tickets look like a wisk of wind in a hurricane compared to what they are selling on the floor. I wish the police would spend some time in respect of these men who are dealing in lottery bonds.
Anyone can go to the banks and get a prospectus which sets out exactly what you must do. Of course the bank itself does not actually sell you the bond. The clerk tells you to go over to the foreign exchange counter where you buy a British pound note for every bond you want and you then mail the pound notes to Great Britain. This whole thing is conducted by the British government through the post office and there are two
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion addresses given: General Post Office, London,
E.C.l and Premium Savings Bond Office, Lytham St. Annes, Lancashire.
Is the Canadian government stopping all the mail going to the General Post Office, London, E.C.l and to the Premium Savings Bond Office, Lytham St. Annes, Lancashire, as it does in connection with Irish sweepstake mail? You cannot use the mail to sell Irish sweepstake tickets. This prospectus points out that the British government will inform the winners of monthly draws by post. Has the Canadian post office no instruction through the Solicitor General to examine mail coming into Canada by post from the British government?
It says in rule 10 on this prospectus that the winners will be notified by post. If the post office is going to stop the mail going to the Irish hospital sweepstakes because this transgresses the postal regulations of Canada, why does it not stop mail going to these addresses in Britain, because this also breaks the laws of this nation?
Far be it from me to ever suggest that the Canadian cabinet should adopt such a sensible idea as a lottery bond so that the people of this nation might have the opportunity of paying off the national debt in a manner that would appeal to many of them. As Mr. Harold Macmillan said in support of Lady Tweedsmuir: If the people are willing to forgo the certainty of interest in order to have a chance of winning a prize each month that is nobody's business but the buyer of the bond.
I cannot see any reason why Canadians should not be given the opportunity of buying Canadian lottery bonds put out by the Canadian government in the same way the British government puts them out, but until the cabinet wakes up and smartens up considerably and introduces such a sweepstake in Canada in order to reduce the Canadian national debt, I simply want to know whether they are going to enforce the law of the land only by chasing bunny girls through taverns and prosecuting stock traders while they flimflam the public on Bay street. Certainly the cabinet ought to prosecute these banks which are issuing the premium savings bonds prospectus, series B, and selling foreign exchange so you can send it to England and get your bonds back by post. Why should we just chase the little bunny girls and leave the bank presidents alone?

9432	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Hon. L. T. Pennell (Solicitor General): Mr. Speaker, as usual the hon. member for York Humber has raised an interesting and novel matter. Unfortunately I have no personal knowledge of these premium savings bonds but I shall have a look into the matter. However, I would point out that the enforcement of the Criminal Code is, generally speaking, a matter exclusively within the

jurisdiction of the provincial authorities. This applies in particular to sections in the Criminal Code relating to gaming and lotteries. I am sure the hon. member will be as pleased as I am to learn that the Department of Justice is completing a study of the sections relating to gaming and lotteries.
